Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement on a question of privilege.
Yesterday morning in the Montreal Gazette, page 13, and in this morning's, page 9, appeared reports signed by Lawrence W. Conroy and entitled respectively "Suspicion in false passport ring points to federal cabinet member," and "Spy aided by false credentials was known as William Brandis".
In February, 1938, Corporal Noel of the R.C.M.P. came to my office and asked me if I did remember recommending one Willy Brandes, who had asked for his naturalization in September, 1936. At first I did not remember, but after the officer had described the applicant I said that I did remember a man, corresponding to the description, who had come to me accompanied by two persons, one of whom I knew well. On was Aaron Marco-vitch, and the other was a gentleman whose name I gave to the police, but I do not need to give it here because he had nothing to do with what happened after that. At the time I was not sure which one of the two had been in my office with Brandes to whom I had given the letter shown to me by the R.C.M.P.
Why did I give this letter? During the election period of 1935 Aaron Marcovitch had presented himself to me as a brother of one Marcovitch whom I knew as a perfect gentleman, and who was in charge of Sam Jacobs' central committee in Cartier division. Aaron told me that he knew the Hebrew element of
[Mr. Graydon.l
my district very well, that he was agent for the Hebrew Sick Benefit Association, which I found to be correct. He succeeded in convincing me of his usefulness. He worked in my committee all through the elections under the supervision of my campaign manager.
The R.C.M.P. officers went to Aaron Marcovitch's house and the latter admitted that the photo of Brandes ivas somewhat familiar but that he could not place the man. He denied having had anything to do with the naturalization papers, and to convince the officers he offered them to go through his records with them. They accepted immediately, and found out the name of Brandes, his certificate number 22970 and the certificate number of one Schulem Brandes, number 10164, a man who had been naturalized in 1913 and who had been given as Willy Brandes' father in the papers showm to me and later presented to the authorities.
Later on Marcovitch admitted that Mrs. Schulem Brandes was an aunt of his own wife, Mrs. Marcovitch.
Willy Brandes' profession was given as Hebrew teacher in the Montreal Hebrew school. I remember that he was a gentleman who was well dressed, spoke very good English and very good French.
The officers found that a marriage appeared to have been celebrated between Willy Brandes and Mary Stern by a certain rabbi- I do not need to give his name-before two witnesses whose names appeared but both of them denied having ever witnessed such a marriage.
When I was told of the details of the R.C.M.P.'s inquiry it helped my memory to reconstruct this affair.
The application forms for naturalization were signed as of the 10th of September, and explained the terms of my letter of the 15th, which is as follows:
Officer in charge of naturalization.
Parliament building,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Sir,
I hereby recommend to you Mr. William Brandes, who is filing his papers to obtain Canadian naturalization. Mr. Brandes has been living in Montreal since he entered Canada at the age of eight years old. He is employed as professor by the Hebrew school of Montreal and is absolutely reeommendable from all angles.
Yours very truly,
(Signed) E.B.
These details of my letter, relating to Brandes' stay in Montreal and his profession of school teacher, had been furnished to me by Marcovitch and Brandes himself who accom-

panied his supposed cousin to my office. These forms showed the number of Brandes' father's naturalization paper obtained in 1913. I had no reason to doubt Marcovitch's words, as he had always acted properly during the time I had known him.
Marcovitch was a very sick man in 1938, when the mounted police made the inquiry, and was restricted in his movements by the said police orders. He died on November 11, 1944.
I never signed anything else but the letter just quoted. Fred Rose's name does not appear in the file. I did not know him until long after September 1936, and to say "that the first signature was that of Rose", which it was necessary to cover by "another signature who would be like Caesar's wife, above suspicion" with all the implications that follow, is malicious and untrue.
I am sorry to have been deceived by Marcovitch and Brandes, whose story was plausible, but there was nothing but absolute good faith in my behaviour. I say again that I have never heard of Fred Rose in this affair.

speechtext: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Acting Minister of Finance! moved the second reading of bill No. 368, to amend the Income War Tax Act.

I am making this speech at the present time because I consider the income tax bill the most appropriate of the measures going through the house in relation to which to make the present submissions. Part of what I have to say would probably have been more appropriate under the foreign exchange control bill; possibly part of it would come appropriately under justice estimates, and part of it under the department of mines. However, in order to save the time of the house I have endeavoured to condense in one speech what I have to say at the moment and to make that speech at this point. I trust, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me a certain latitude in my remarks if in part the material I give to the house is not strictly relevant to the Income War Tax Act. As I have said, I am endeavouring, for the purpose of saving time, to make three speeches in one.
The first part of my remarks deals with the effect on the Canadian economy; of parity of the Canadian dollar; the second deals with the measures taken by the government to overcome the loss sustained by the
mining industry, while the third offers some recommendations concerning the gold mining industry and the free gold market generally.
When this government, in the wisdom of the experts of the Department of Finance, decided to put the Canadian dollar at parity, certain definite things happened. The first, and probably from the long-time point of view the most serious, was the restriction placed upon our exports. We have recently heard at great length the comparison of Canadian costs with costs elsewhere, particularly in the United States, and it has been strongly impressed upon this country and upon this parliament that Canada must export to live. Canadian manufacturing costs are higher than those in the United States, despite the fact that wages are lower in Canada. The selling price of the finished product is higher in Canada. Therefore Canadian sales aoroad will have to overcome two very serious handicaps imposed upon them by the economy of the country.
The ten per cent discount on Canadian currency was a help to Canadian producers, and to remove it at this critical time was a blow to all industry. I mention in particular at this time the Canadian lumber industry, and I should like to quote one paragraph from United States News of July 26 with reference to that industry. The article deals with what is called currency tinkering. I quote:
A hazard is involved in currency tinkering. Widespread upward valuations of currencies mav promise a temporary buying advantage in the* United States markets, but eventually when foreign business men must sell in United States markets those countries might be left high and dry. Right now, by raising currency values, foreign countries can buy more cheaply and sell more dearly in United States markets; but the time may come when they would like to reverse the situation. Canada can now sell lumber to this country at almost any price, but ivhen the present abnormal demand subsides Canadian timber may cost too much for United States buyers simply because United States dollars cost too much.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the condition of one of our primary industries and I suggest that it is not uncommon in many other primary industries. Certain industries have been able to raise their selling prices in the United States but many of them find it difficult to do so for reasons of our internal economy and for reasons that are basic because of our higher unit costs.
If the pattern of the industrial market is at all similar to the pattern of the previous cycles, we are approaching the end of a boom market. There is a distinct possibility that we may be going into a period of declining markets and production, with the usual dis-
Income War Tax

location of employment and the troubles that it always brings. I ray this because of the study I have recently made of the world markets, and particularly the markets on this continent. The graph shows an unmistakably similar pattern to that of both the 1920 crash and the one subsequent to that, just prior to the war. Therefore I say to the government that it is vitally important that they should not throw away at this time any possibility of strengthening our trading position.
There is one thing more I should like to say on parity of the Canadian dollar with the United States dollar. It is but a dream; it is not in fact in existence. There may be an official quotation of the foreign exchange control board, but in actual fact Canadian funds are selling at anywhere from 3^ per cent to per cent discount at this hour. That is not in a small way; it is not in the small banks. I wish to quote the middle of the market as quoted to me by the Chase National bank, the National City bank and the Bankers Trust, three of the largest banks certainly in New York, and probably in the .entire United States, if not in the world. These are the quotations of the middle market in recent United States dollar terms: August 5, T619-that is what they would pay for a Canadian dollar; August 6, T637; August 7, -9662; August 8, -9650; August 9, -9656. and August 11, yesterday, the quoting is the other way. Our currency was selling at a discount of over 3J per cent.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I received a letter from Chicago the other day which showed that a man whom I knew slightly was able to buy a very large sum of Canadian currency from one of the Canadian banks at over a three per cent discount rate. Therefore parity does not in fact exist, and the government will have to take recognition of it, because from time to time the pressure on the Canadian dollar will be greater and greater owing to the fact that normal trade between the countries is no longer in existence. I mention this particularly because, except in the tourist season, our normal trade with United States, which is largely agricultural, has been considerably curtailed since the period of the war. That has been brought about because we are sending most of our agricultural produce to the countries of Europe and. the United Kingdom. Therefore it is reasonable to expect that even after the 3| per cent discount the Canadian currency will only be-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am endeavouring to do that. I want to point out why I consider that the taxation proposed by this measure is a severe blow on the mining companies, and that the relief suggested by this government is in fact of little value. I want to show the house, and I hope the country, that the blow suffered not only by mining but by the whole Canadian economy is brought about by the move which the government has taken and that parity is in itself a taxation of Canadian production.
At the beginning of my remarks I said that I was doing this in order to save the time of the house. I could have made this speech on the Foreign Exchange Control Act, but I refrained from doing it because I spoke to the minister about it and he suggested that I make one speech at this time. However, 1 shall endeavour to obey your ruling.
I have just one more word on this business of parity. Canadian currency is selling at widely separated ooints in the United States to-day at as much as seventeen and twenty per cent discount. I understand that even the Trans-Canada Air Lines agents are charging as much as six per cent discount. I refer to the agents to whom Trans-Canada Air Lines sends people in New York.
So much for parity; now let us see what this has meant to the rest of the Canadian economy, particularly mining. In Canada we were the first to boost our currency. Several other countries followed suit, Sweden and Brazil being the last. We did that along with Sweden, Brazil and other countries because we wished to buy in the only market-where goods were plentiful and at as cheap a rate as possible. In other words we tried to put our buying position high and paid little attention to our selling position; but we shall have to take recognition of that, and very soon.
Now I come to the question of taxation. Putting the currency at par has meant a loss to the Canadian gold producer and the Canadian producer of base metals with a large gold content, of ten per cent of the gross value of his product. In other words he did not lose ten per cent of his profit; he lost far more than that. He lost ten per cent of the gross value, and in some cases

Income War Tax
that means the entire profit. That should be very clearly understood by this house. It was a percentage of the gross value that was taken away, not the net value. The government has brought in some small measure of relief, and in a moment or two I am going to give figures to show how extremely negligible that relief is, but first I want to speak briefly about the situation in South Africa and Australia.
In South Africa the Union government under the minister of finance, Mr. Hofmeyr, realized the importance of producing every ounce of gold they could. So they arranged a method of differential taxation for low grade ore. In other words, if 1 can explain it to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house, this is what they do. There is a rate of taxation on the mine; but for the low grade ore the depletion allowance is increased as the grade decreases. In other words the depletion allowance goes up in inverse ratio 'to the grade of the ore. That means that as your grade goes down, so does your taxation go down, so eventually on ore which is definitely marginal and where the cost of milling and mining is very little less than the gold recovered is worth, the depletion allowance approaches one hundred per cent. I have not seen the most recent figures, but I understand that the rate goes very high, and I have heard that in some cases there is actually a bonus on the production of low-grade ore.
What does this do? It assists a mine with a large body of low grade ore to take out that ore body almost without taxation, and that is a tremendous gain to the economy of any country; for it means that instead of so many thousand tons of rock lying under the ground you have so many hundred ounces of gold. For years the mining industry have pledged with this government and with the Department of Finance to increase the depletion allowance to fifty per cent for both shareholder and mining corporation, but nothing has been done. I want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that careful study should be given by this government, if they are sincere in wanting to help the mines, to the South African method of taxation as I have endeavoured to explain it.
In Australia a situation existed similar to that which exists in Canada to-day. A government not particularly helpful to the mines was in power-I think it was during the Lang regime-and a heavy taxation was put on Australian gold mining. This effectively killed all the mines in eastern Australia, that is in New South Wales and Victoria, and those mines have never reopened. They were small producers, but they were very helpful in the development of the country in that agriculture followed the mines into the hinterland of those two states, where now a thriving agricultural economy exists. We have a close parallel to that right here in Quebec, where we have low grade mines just getting by, making profits of a few cents a ton. For 1944 the average profit of all western Quebec gold producers was 62 cents a ton. Those mines will do everything they can'to keep in production, but if they are forced to close it will be found impossible to continue agricultural development along that northern Quebec clay belt, because the mines provide the market in that area. If that market is taken away from agriculture it will find itself badly off, because other markets are too far away. So to have the mines close would be a definite hindrance to colonization in that part of Quebec. Just the other day, in connection with a railway bill, we saw the difficulties that exist in connection with colonization and the important part played by the mines.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to what the government's proposals mean to a group of individual mines. Putting the Canadian dollar at parity reduced the gross value of the product of our gold mines by ten per cent. Now let us see what the proposals of the Department of Finance mean to a group of low grade mines; and I have the figures here for twelve low grade mines in Ontario. With the consent of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put this table on the record. If I have that permission I need only read the name of the mine, the grade in ounces per ton, the net profit per ton and what the new proposals of the Department of Finance mean per ton to each of these producers

Now, let us look at the figures for two mines in Quebec, namely Canadian Malartic and East Malartic. The figures in the daily press for Canadian Malartic show the grade at about $3.80 a ton; and therefore on parity Canadian Malartic will lose at the rate of 38 cents per ton. The proposals by the minister have been worked out by the mines to show a magnificent saving of $SOO a year in this mine. The 1945 figures for East Malartic show a saving of precisely nothing. We have heard these figures brought into the house and the statement that they give assistance to the Canadian mining economy. The figures I have just read for two provinces show that they mean nothing. In fact, I wondered at the minister, who is a sensible man, reading them into the record. Surely the department must have been putting one over on him on that score.
One more quotation about mining costs. Mr. Drummond-Hay of Winnipeg who, I believe, is the managing director of San Antonio and God's Lake, speaking recently in Winnipeg said that the concessions are of infinitesimal value.
I say this situation is extremely critical for the mining industry, because once a mine closes, particularly a low-grade mine, it does not open again. Once a mine closes-and hundreds of mines have closed across Canada- Mr. ABBOTT: Hundreds which should never have been opened, perhaps, too.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not referring to producing mines.

And there are hundreds of producing mines which have closed. The figures given the house a few weeks ago by the hon. member for York South showed twenty or. thirty mines which opened, produced and closed without paying anything to their shareholders. But those mines paid a considerable amount in taxation to the economy of this country, to say nothing about the gold they produced. I believe it was in the neighbourhood of $30 million or $40 million in gold they produced, and yet not me cent was returned to the shareholders.
The government's proposals are negligible. Now we are faced with two things, the first of which is that Canadian currency is selling at a discount to-day in New York. If the government are adamant in maintaining parity -and I do not know whether they can change their minds again-the Canadian gold producers must be given the benefit of the open market buying rate in the principal American banks.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The hon. member said he did not know whether the government would change its mind. Is he in favour of putting the Canadian dollar back to a discount?
' Mr. ADAMSON: Not at the present time, because you cannot continuously juggle currency.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I was wondering about that, because the hon. member implied that the government might change its mind again to help the gold miners.

I see no reason for the government's having taken this action, namely, that of putting the dollar at parity. But once it is done, it cannot continuously play around with currency. The government in its wisdom has followed a course which I consider a wrong one. It has taken a step which will seriously affect the entire Canadian economy, an effect which the government cannot make stick. The government cannot maintain Canadian currency at par with the United States dollar. The fact that the buying rate to-day is 3i per cent discount and is increasing, shows that it cannot do so. Therefore the first thing I ask the government to do to assist the mines is to see to it that they get the benefit of the discount on Canadian currency. At the present time it amounts to 3i per cent, or over a dollar per ounce of gold.
The second thing I ask the government to do is to increase the depletion allowance, particularly on low-grade mines. What they liave done amounts to nothing. I suggest the system which originated in Africa, whereby depletion allowance could be worked out as an inverse ratio with the value of the ore treated.
The next thing-and I have no time to discuss it in detail now-is that the mining companies should be allowed to sell on an established free market for gold in Canada, or do their own marketing of their own bullion in markets elsewhere. I say this because there is no doubt that the market is able to absorb our production. Since 1939, according to the American bureau of metal statistics-[DOT] and this is the last quotation I want to make -the world production of gold has been
240,019,000	fine ounces. This figure includes estimates of 29,000,000 for Russia and Siberia, and 12,700,000 for Korea and Japan. All other figures are from official sources. Presumably, figures for the seven year period from September 1, 1939 to September 1, 1946 would be comparable in amount. In other words, since the outbreak of war the world has produced $8,400,000,000 worth of gold at $35 per ounce, and at the same time gold holdings of the
Income War Tax

United States government have been reduced, according to official reports by some $2,500,000,000. It is evident, therefore, that the world ex-United States has absorbed some $11,000,000,000 worth of gold since September 1, 1939. . It seems reasonable to suppose that many of the present owners of this metal paid a premium for it in terms of currencies including United States dollars. If they had thought that gold was not worth more than $35 United States dollars per ounce, many of them would have bought dollars instead of the metal. The United States government has made it impossible for their citizens to acquire gold as a means of preserving value in the face of a depreciating dollar, which the rest of the world has recognized by outbidding the United States government for some 300,000,000 ounces.
Now, Mr. Speaker, our maximum production of gold is in the neighbourhood of $200,000.000 a year. Since the war the United States alone have lost more gold than our total production. For anybody to say that we could not market our total gold production is, in view of these figures, nonsense. Therefore I say, if you are serious in seeking to maintain the gold industry in Canada, provide an opportunity for the operating mines to market their bullion how and where they wish, increase the depletion allowance to at least fifty per cent and possibly more on marginal producers, and immediately allow the Canadian producer to obtain the benefit of the discount already in existence on Canadian currency in the United States.
Mr. JOSEPH A. BRADETTE (Cochrane): Mr. Speaker, I am sorry in a way to have to take the time of the house at this stage of the session, but I believe it is my implicit duty to present the situation as I see it of the gold mining industry. I happen to represent a constituency where for the past thirty-five years there has been the greatest development in gold mining, and as this bill deals with and may bring some relief to the industry, I believe it is my duty to say a few words.
I am voicing the sentiments of every one of my constituents when I state that we were not merely satisfied but proud when the government brought the Canadian dollar on a parity with the United States dollar. We produce gold, pulp-wood, wood pulp, sulphite and newsprint in northern Ontario. At least ninety per cent of our production goes to the United States, and so we were benefiting when the United States dollar was at a ten per cent premium over the Canadian dollar. But we always thought in terms of the
fMr. Adamson.]
national economy, of what was good for Canada as a whole. We are proud of the fact that the Canadian dollar to-day is the soundest monetary unit in the world, and I say that without fear of contradiction.
But one industry, gold mining was hit when the Canadian dollar was placed on a parity with the United States dollar. This industry was hit an unexpected blow; it was a bolt from the blue. For the last four or five years our gold mining industry has been getting a price of $38.50 an ounce for gold, not $35,00, and we must never lose sight of that fact in discussing this important question. But because of the ten per cent premium on the United States dollar our gold mining industry has been able to build up and expand on that price for gold. They have been developing new mines and putting them, into operation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) so well realized the position of the gold mining industry that when he made his announcement in the House of Commons that the Canadian dollar was on a parity with the United' States dollar he singled out the gold mining industry as one that would be hit by that policy. The very night he made his announcement I received telegrams from some of the industrialists of Kapuskasing, Smooth Rock Falls, and Iroquois Falls. They were worried over what it meant to the industry. However, the price for newsprint, lumber and pulpwood is not set by Washington; it is not a standard price, and I told these industrialists that I was positive that the price situation was so resilient that they would get an increased price for their production. A few days later the price of newsprint was raised to $6.50 per ton, and the wartime prices and trade board also raised the price of lumber for export to the United States.
I want to deal with an industry that has played a great role in our Canadian national economy. Under war conditions the gold mining industry is one of the first victims, because immediately there is a shortage of man-power and of the necessary materials for continuing their operations as in peace time. This applied just as forcibly in world war II as in world war I. if not more so. Very soon after the outbreak of war in 1939, and more particularly.in 1940, the gold mining industry felt a great shortage of man-power because a large number of the men engaged in the industry enlisted voluntarily in world war II just as they did in world war I, and in a very short time there was also a great shortage of the materials required in the industry. Under those* conditions the production of gold decreased to some extent.

Income War Tax
In 1941, if I remember right, the Minister of Finance appealed to the gold mining industry for intensive production so as to help our Canadian credit position, more particularly in the United States market. [DOT] There was an immediate response to that appeal from the gold mining industry. They delved deeply into their ore reserves, so that to-day many of the big producers find their ore reserves greatly depleted-and if there is one thing that causes the management of a mine to worry it is the depletion of their ore reserve. No matter what some members of parliament may think, no one is more concerned in lengthening the life of a mine than the mine owners themselves. It is true that mining is a wasting process, that eventually you are left with a hole in the ground with no more ore or work to be done. At present in Canada there are many abandoned towns which in the past were thriving communities. But that does not mean that there has been waste in the development of these mines. I hold no brief for the mine owners, but I have seen the mines in operation and I know that the mine owners have spent all their energies in producing all the gold they could possibly find.
There was great rejoicing when a few years ago the price of gold was increased to S35 an ounce. The reason for that rejoicing was that it meant that a mine like Hollinger, in the town of Timmins, had its life lengthened by at least thirty years. I want the house to be seized of this fact, that no mine operators and no mine owners that I know of are deliberately wasting the resources and natural assets of their mines.
Having established that point I would like hon. members to realize what the gold mining industry means to our section of the country. I am divulging no secret when I say that only a few days ago the leader of the Social Credit party, after visiting northern Quebec, said that he was astonished to find what the gold mining industry of northern Quebec and northern Ontario meant to those sections of the country and also to the whole of Canada. Around these gold mines have grown up centres of population such as Kirkland Lake, Timmins, Schumacher, South Porcupine and many olhers, which enjoy public utility services and social services which have been permanently established because the people expect to remain there for a long period of time, in fact all their life. Again I repeat that management and labour are working together in the closest co-operation possible to produce every ton of ore and by that process to extend the life of the mines, and that not a single ton of it is
being wasted. I would not fight for one moment for any so-called gold mine in which the grades of ore were so low that it would not be economical to exploit them. Yesterday I was speaking to a young member of parliament from Amos, Quebec. He spoke of a particular mine in that section in which the cost of operations is $40 an ounce, and I told him that he could not expect anyone to fight for such a mine, because after all we cannot afford to bonus mines that are not self-supporting on the basis of the prices that are being received at the present time.
Owing to the increased price we were getting, by reason of the difference between United States and Canadian currency, we have permitted the construction and operation of a large number of low-grade mines, operating on the basis of a price of $38.50 an ounce, and these mines were barely existing, making very little profit. Those are the mines now in. operation which we want to see maintained. We do not want to see hundreds if not thousands of men who are at present gainfully employed thrown out of employment.
There is more involved in gold mining than the bare extraction of the gold. In the clay belt of northern Ontario gold mining has made a considerable difference to the Canadian economy from the point of view of agriculture. Without gold mining we would not have gone ahead to the extent that we have done in colonization and agriculture, and it might be a revelation to members of parliament to learn that in the last thirty-two years in northern Ontario, in that part of the country I represent, there has been a greater advance and a greater influx of new population engaging in agricultural activities than in any other section of Canada, including the west. Not only do these conditions give employment to farmers in providing them with a local market for all their production, but there has also been a remarkable development in our forest industries as well. These factors alone will cause everyone to realize how necessary it is to maintain at capacity the gold mining industry of Canada. The industry means so much to our national economy. In my opinion the situation that has been created by the parity of the Canadian dollar is in one way a good thing, because it will make members of parliament more conscious of our gold mining industry and of some of its problems.
I remember in 1934 when the prime minister of that day. Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, in his budget speech, made the announcement of the bullion taxation on gold, and I was the only member to rise immediately and assure him that, knowing the situation as I did, it
Income War Tax

would be impossible to apply that tax. But I got little applause at the time. I have no wish to be critical, but I suggest that there are very few members of parliament who know the exact situation and fully realize what it means to our national life to have a prosperous gold mining industry.
I would not, of course, say that the proposals brought forward by the government are entirely satisfactory.
The same officials were in the Department of Finance then as now, and I am afraid they are responsible for both these bad things.
Even if they are, I must say to the hon. member-
I fought against the bullion tax too.

I am sure that those same gentlemen, knowing the situation as well as they do, were the first to realize that a mistake had been made. We must realize that we are dealing with people who are completely open-minded. I for one do not believe that an official of the government, with the wide experience that these men have had and the admirable work they have done since the beginning of the war-work that has been a revelation to the entire world-would deliberately do anything that would hamper the gold mining industry, or for that matter any other industry.
There is another important thing about gold mining which I would draw to the attention of the house. I would point out, by the way, how important it is that the men at the head of the industry have been so practical. I deplore some of the criticism that has appeared in the press, and I have in mind one newspaper in particular. I will not mention its name, but I will say that most of its arguments are far-fetched, and it goes too far. I say that because gold mining, I believe, has a good case, and for that reason we do not need to overdo it in its presentation. I know that the big mining men will not be severely critical but will be constructive in this instance as they have been in the past. I should like to quote one or two statements that have appeared in the press, and I do so to corroborate what I have been saying. Let me first quote something that was said in Winnipeg, as taken from the Ottawa Journal:
Winnipeg, July 29-(CP). The proposed dominion relief to gold mines to compensate for the loss suffered when Canadian dollars were brought to parity with the United States has been approved by mining men and Manitoba mines department officials, but it is not enough.

This is fair criticism, and at the same time it is constructive. It shows a realization that the government has been taking a step in the right direction. I quote again:
J. P. de Wet, secretary of the Manitoba chamber of mines, said any relief would be welcome but present relief does not come up to expectations. Provincial director of mines Doctor G. M. Furnival said although no Manitoba mine was in danger of having to shut down due to exchange loss, the relief would encourage some prospective mining operations.
This again is constructive. May I now quote one paragraph from an article that appeared in Saturday Night of August 10. This is just a few lines to give hon. members an idea of the situation:
One of the much talked of recessions in the recent mining market which suffered devastating losses following the placing of the Canadian dollar on par with the U.S. dollar, was that in the shares of Giant Yellowknife Gold Mines. It was a market in which for weeks a terrific beating W'as taken, particularly in the shares of prospects, the newer mines, or those where production could be visualized and Giant-one of Canada's potentially big gold mines-declined close to the $5 mark, less than half of the high attained by the shares in 1945.
When the announcement was made in the house by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a few days ago, the Globe and Mail made a statement that suggests that there must have been a leak somewhere, because mining stocks sky-rocketed. I do not know what figure they received, but the first information I had was that there was a bonus of $2 an ounce on all our gold production. I was wrong on that point. I have no sympathy with the stock market, because if inquiry is made under certain conditions, when it becomes bearish, it is evident that somebody is holding the bag for the speculators, and I have no sympathy with speculators. My sympathy is for the producers, the promoters, the prospectors and those who do the actual work, but I have none for those who try to make money without taking any of the risks. I quote again:
The price of the shares at time of writing had improved and this was partly due to the federal government's new ruling authorizing exemption from taxation for new mines for a three-year period.
There is a mine that is developing low-grade ore, and these people are satisfied that the government has tried to help them.
I wish now to say a few words about a world market for gold. Personally I do not believe in it, because under present conditions I do not think it is practical. I will go further than that. If the mining industry as a body will come to the federal government and say, "IVe are willing to take all the risks

Income War Tax
of selling in the open market. We are paid by the federal treasury at the standard price set by Washington, but to-day we believe there are other markets where we can get more for our gold, and we want to take the risks involved in that market", then I suggest that the government might act. But unless those engaged in the industry are organized and willing and ready to do this, I do not support that principle.
We talk about prices being paid by Mexico. I wish to tell hon. members that the price which the producer would get from Mexico would be less than $35 an ounce. I know whereof I speak. The same thing applies to Argentina. There again, although the price seems to be a big one from here, when you study the situation and get the proper information you will realize that the producer would get less than S34 for an ounce for gold.
We talk about outside markets like India or Egypt, which are in the sterling area. Should our producers take a chance of disturbing their markets by entering the sterling area? I just leave these thoughts for the consideration of hon. members. I do not know of any big producers who are in favour of that. I did not hear Mr. Bickell or Mr. Longmoire or the men who are well versed in gold mining and in the marketing of gold come out very strongly for an open market for our production. If they were asking for a guarantee, or rather governmental protection, to have access to the world market, then its effect would be destroyed by this demand. At the moment there are guarantees of a standard price for gold on which we can implicitly rely, and that is an important factor in any kind of an industry and in any kind of a mine. Again I leave that to the consideration of the House of Commons.
So far as I am personally concerned I am not convinced that an open market for our gold would be the proper thing to have. Are we going to try to bootleg or black-market one of the things which has set the monetary standard of the world? Are we to take the risk with Washington, for instance, after finding out that we were able to improve our production? The attitude of Washington has been a stabilizing factor for the past four or five years, in fact for a long period of time; and at times we have got a premium of $3.50 an ounce on the gold produced. Are we going to throw that overboard, practically destroy that security of marketing, and try out what appears green from a distance but on close examination proves to be nothing but shallows so far as our production is concerned?
I shall now say a word about depletion allowance. A lot could be said on this subject, 63260-297
but I know that hon. members have read the fine report and the recommendations made by the senate committee on natural resources. Depletion allowance has been the bone of contention for a number of years, and even if it were increased to fifty per cent it would not be the solution of all these problems. But no matter what may be said, the offer of the government to allow the option of accepting as depletion either 33^ per cent of net profits or $2 per ounce of gold produced is a step in the right direction, and it is going to help a lot of low grade ore mines. However, I wish to make a special request of the government. I do not believe that $2 an ounce as an option is sufficient. I believe that the amount should be $2.50 at least. In placing the amount at $2.50 you are not going to help the big producers; generally speaking they look after themselves. They have shown in the past that they can do it, and they are showing it at the present time. It is the marginal producer, the one on the borderline, that I am worrying about-the one I mentioned a few moments ago. These mines exist to a great extent in northern Ontario and more particularly in northern Quebec.
I repeat that the option of $2 an ounce is helping at the present time, regardless of what the previous speaker may have said. I could quote all kinds of statistics tb corroborate my statement, but I make this sincere appeal to the treasury and to the Minister of Finance. The amount should be $2.50 instead of $2. I speak with experience, and I believe that my word should be listened to. I am speaking not in the name of the gold mining industry only; they do not want self-pity. They have always come back on their feet and they will do it in the present crisis; at all times they showed a great deal of self reliance. But this is almost a crisis for them. Let us place ourselves in the position of the gold mining industry so far as parity of the Canadian dollar is concerned, and we shall see the reasons for their uneasiness and why they are not feeling so happy, why they are afraid that the expansion which they have in mind during the rehabilitation and post-war era will be stultified.
I do not wish to enlarge on this subject because I realize the impatience of the house after so many months of arduous work; however, I am speaking with all the sincerity I possess. I should be the last one to fight for any organization which did not deserve it, but I have seen with my own eyes and I know what it means, not only regionally but also nationally, to maintain in its integrity the gold mining institutions of our country. It

Income War Tax

was a marvellous thing for me during the depression years when everyone of us suffered so grievously. There is not a member of parliament, or a Canadian worthy of the name, who did not try to help during those five or six horrible years when we had so many people come to us with their tale of woe. Even in the agricultural centres there were depressions. But when you went to the gold mining centres you found the people fully employed. People came there from every section of Canada. To the credit of the gold mining industry of this country there was no decrease in wages, although there was an oversaturated labour supply and thousands of men who wanted to work in the mines. But more than that, during those years the companies found it possible to improve the working conditions of their workers and to some extent to increase their wages.
It is my good privilege to know a number of mine owners, and I have seen them in action. There is one thing I have against the mine management and the mine owners, namely, that they have not told their fine records, achievements and story to the Canadian people. For instance, they have not told what they have done for the treatment and the cure of silicosis. Owing to the work carried on by the mine owners, in a few short years silicosis will be non-existent in this country. The mine owners have improved the working conditions, and have done all they possibly could for the workers generally. There is not a mine manager or a superintendent in my section of the country that a man when he leaves his shift or the level on which he works could not go and speak to. I am not saying that everything has been perfect but I am asking that due consideration be given to an industry which means so much to all walks of life-to agriculture, to manufacturers, to our labourers and also to our national economy. They have always played the game. They do not ask anything that is unfair or unpracticable. I know that the department is fully seized of the situation. The remedies which have been brought forward will help, and no doubt something more can and will be done. If that help is given I can assure the house that the districts for whom I speak and the fine population that is involved will highly appreciate it, as will every other section of our country.

Speaking for this group at this particular time, on second reading of the bill, I shall be just as brief as possible. We do not agree with the principle of this bill. Of course the minister -[DOT]id not expect us to agree with it, and he 
knows the sections with which we disagree. I hope that he can understand some of the provisions with which we disagree. I do not think there is a lawyer in this chamber to-day who can interpret what the government means by some of them.
The minister told me at one time that I had no legal training. I have none, but I am sure I could put down what I meant in better words than are contained in the bill, even if I wanted to cover up my meaning. They have successfully covered up everything that they intended to mean. They have made it possible to interpret this bill in any way they wish. In my opinion this bill is for no other purpose than to liquidate and prevent the development of this working class organization, the cooperative movement, the best free enterprise organization in Canada to-day. I have set out emphatically our opinions and what we think of this bill. I do not suppose there is the slightest hope of convincing the acting minister, the minister himself or their sharp advisers in the department about these things, but I want to try to convince the house, and I am sorry that the two hon. members who gave the particular illustration that I am going to use are not in their places.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) is over in the industrial relations committee; the hon. member for Halifax was in the chamber but went out. I am going to use the illustration given by the hon. member for Calgary West to indicate what we mean when we say there is no profit in a cooperative enterprise.
The illustration given by the hon. gentleman was that of a stranger driving along a road, who decides he needs some supplies. He comes to a little settlement on the road, and stops. There is a store over here belonging, we will say, to Mr. A, and a store on the other side of the road belonging to the local cooperative association. He looks at both stores. They appear exactly the same; to the stranger there is no apparent difference. Both sell the same goods, and both have the same window display. But bear this in mind: those stores were not put there for the benefit of that stranger. They were put there by Mr. A and the cooperative association primarily to serve the people of that community. The stranger travelling over the road is only a casual customer, who may never come that way again, while those stores were put there to give service to the community.
When Mr. A runs his store, everything he has left over and above the cost is profit for his pocket, and he uses that profit for his living. That is quite legitimate; there is nothing wrong with it.

All right; I shall get to that. He is an individual; so am I as a member of the cooperative. Do not forget that members of cooperative associations as individuals will pay taxes with just as good or bad grace as anyone else, according to their nature. I do not like paying my taxes. I pay them with a kind of brassy smile, as when I lose at poker, but I pay them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Poker? You mean cribbage.

Right. Now I want to point out that this individual, Mr. A, to supply his own household, buys his groceries or clothing or hardware from his store, but he does not put money in the till for that. Neither do his clerks, if he has any. They take what stuff they buy at the wholesale price, as a general practice, or with a very little added to cover the cost of moving it over the counter, but without paying any profit. So Mr. A makes no profit on Mr. A's personal business. Get that point, please. Over on the other side of the road is the store owned by the cooperative association of which I am a member. A hundred other people in that community, farmers and workers of one kind or another, are my partners. We felt we could save ourselves some money; our incomes were not large and we wanted to make them go as far as possible in the purchase of supplies. So we decided that while no one of us could build a store of his own, all of us together could build one which would belong to all of us, and that we did. To that extent the one hundred partners in this cooperative association became one entity as far as the ownership of the store was concerned. When we go in to buy our stuff we are in exactly the same position as Mr. A. We can make no profit on our own business.
I want to make that point clear, because we are distinctly dissatisfied with this bill on that account. No distinction is made in the bill between a cooperative association and a private concern. There is no place in the bill under which a cooperative association can feel safe in going ahead with the particular kind of enterprise or industry in which it is engaged. The whole thing is an endeavour to put the cooperative association in exactly the same position as everybody else. Do not forget the illustration. No man can make profit from his own purchases in his own place of business, whether he be a gold miner -and we heard a g*od deal of talk about gold this morning-or a storekeeper or an elevator operator or anything else. He cannof make 63260-297J
money supplying himself from his own stocks. He makes his profit when he supplies other people who pay him more than he has had to pay for the goods or services he supplies. That is his income. It is a legitimate income, and I am not complaining about it. I am pointing out that as far as we in a cooperative are concerned, we make no profit for ourselves.
When I rose I said I would not take any more of the time of the house than was necessary. We are not going to let this bill pass in committee without questioning a number of sections, but as far as this particular stage is concerned all I have tried to make clear is that we do not agree with this legislation.

Speaking on the foreign exchange bill on Friday last the acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had this to say, at page 4530 of Hansard:
If we were part of the United States of course we would not be faced with all these difficulties; we would all have the same currency. But on balance we are a debtor nation, and to a very considerable extent. If we are to retain our national integrity and the integrity of our dollar, we have to adopt appropriate measures to see that our exchange position is protected.
I can think of nothing that will protect our exchange position and protect the Canadian economy more than the encouragement of the gold mining industry of this country. During the last few days the minister may have noticed in the press that in spite of the urgency of the situation and the desire for gold on the part of the government, there has been a decrease in the production, which decrease is rapidly becoming more pronounced because of high costs of production. Since 1910, Canada has developed perhaps the most efficient mining industry in the world, with the result that much ore which ordinarily would be waste rock has become of economic value and can be treated at a profit, even though the profit be small. If this industry is to continue to play a part in the economic life of the country, the government must give some encouragement to keep Canadian gold mines in production. The acting minister and his departmental officials must know that once it is necessary to close a mine down because of the grade of the ore or because conditions do not warrant carrying on, the cost of reopening that mine is so great that few mines ever reopen.
During the depression the mining industry, as I have stated before in this house, was the [DOT] one industry able to carry the country through. Again in the early days of the war, when the government wanted United States exchange rather than to go on lend-lease, they appealed
Income War Tax

to the mining companies to increase production, which the mining companies were only too glad to do in spite of the fact that they had to pay much heavier taxes. During the last two years there has been intense activity in this country in connection with gold mining. There has been a great deal of diamond drilling, and many new prospects have been lined up for development in the days to come. A great many of these prospects are in the province of Quebec and in the northern part of Ontario. I am afraid the policy which has been announced by the minister is going to have the result that many of these prospects, because of their location, and the grade of their ore, will not be brought into production- not because the mining people have no faith in their industry, but because the expense of bringing a mine into production is so great that there must be some assurance there will be a return of the capital so invested.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) pointed out that since the government placed our money on a parity with the United States dollar there has been fluctuation in exchange of about four per cent. It seems to me the minister and his officials are not giving the gold producers even the world price for the gold they produce. They say to the mining industry: We will be very generous with you and give you back this twenty cents an ounce which we have been overcharging you in refining charges for the last few years, but we will refrain from giving you the world price for your product.
I suggest the minister should do what his department did before the war. At that time when a mine sent its bullion to the mint it received the mean of exchange for the day on which the bullion was received at the mint, the day before and the day after. This would result in a mine receiving at least a portion of the $3.50 which was taken away from it when the government decided to place our money on a parity with that of the United States. If departmental officials have checked thoroughly into the relief they are giving, by way of either the 33J per cent depletion or the $2 an ounce, they will have realized that very few mines in Canada benefit to any extent.
I would make particular reference to one mine with which I am connected, where we received back $400 a month or about $5,000 a year on account of the reduction in handling charges. The production of the mine is approximately 40.000 ounces of gold a year. This means that $140,000 is taken away from the mine at $3.50 per ounce and $5,000 is returned by way of mint charges.

I suggest to the minister that the manner in which he explained' this question of relief to the people of Canada gave the impression that the government was giving relief to extent of $2 an ounce on gold produced. The feeling has got around that the mines are being penalized only to the extent of $1.50 an ounce, whereas actually the mines are being penalized to the extent of the whole of the $3 50.
I suggest to the minister that in a near marginal mine, where costs equalled $35 per ounce prior to the reduction of $3.50 per ounce of gold, the operations now become marginal, the net profit is nil, and as a result no depletion of any kind applies. Hence the $2 an ounce alternative depletion is an empty gesture. As the hon. member for York West pointed out, in some cases it amounts only to one cent per ton of ore passing through the mill. I think it would be a tragic thing for this country, and I am sure the minister and his officials agree with me, if the industry which has meant so much to Canada in the past, and which will mean just as much in the future, is allowed to deteriorate to the point where many mines have to close up. Because as sure as we sit in this House of Commons to-day, the cycle of trade and commerce moves. Days of depression will, unfortunately arise; and when those days come the government of Canada once again will want every ounce of gold produced that the industry can possibly produce.
I believe the government should allow the base metal mines to market all their products at the world price. I see no reason why Canadian mines should be penalized as they are now. I would point out that in the early days of the war, Canadian metal mines made contracts with the British and Canadian governments to sell their total production at the price level which then existed. Those contracts the mines faithfully carried out, with the result that the British and Canadian governments saved vast sums of money at the expense of the metal mines of Canada. These prices were maintained in spite of the fact that there were tremendous increases in costs. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) say that the mining industry was determined to carry on, because I am positive that that is a fact. But in spite of that determination I feel sure there will be many casualties along the road, and that many mines will have to close down if the present intention of the government is carired through.
That is not the only factor. I feel that many operations will never come into existence. I know of two properties where decisions have been made to hold the development over for

Income War Tax
another year. One has to remember that the mining industry employs many men behind the lines to keep the mines in operation. If the minister and his officials cannot see their way clear to remedy this situation to-day, then I fear that many men employed in industry throughout Canada will be put out of employment.
I appeal to the acting minister and his officials to do something forthwith to remedy this situation. Only the other day I was speaking to the president of some low-grade mines in Quebec, and he told me that he was going to attempt to carry on, but just how long he could do so under existing circumstances he did not know, because his profit, which stood around forty cents before the government decided on parity, had disappeared. Only one of his mines makes any profit to-day.
I appeal to the minister to study this whole question, and to give relief. I suggest he do what has been requested by mining associations throughout Canada-give back to the mines that fifty per cent depletion allowance, both to the operating companies and to the shareholders.
The dominion government takes tremendous taxation from the mines, and puts nothing into them. In one district of which I have knowledge, the Pickle Crow area, the dominion government has taken almost $4 million in taxes and has put nothing into the area, despite the fact that requests have been made for assistance in transportation and in other ways.
I suggest that the acting minister or his officials should have a talk with Mr. Justice Davis, the High Commissioner for Australia. In Australia they believe that gold mines should be encouraged one hundred per cent. If my information is correct, they do not tax them, although I am not making that suggestion here. I do suggest however that some assistance be given.
I should like to say something about the apparent leak to which reference was made by the hon. member for Cochrane. If one studies the graphs of the Toronto stock exchange and the Montreal stock exchange for five days prior to the minister's announcement, he will notice that on the Monday prior to the minister's statement, selling started and continued during the whole week. On the afternoon prior to the announcement, which was made at eight o'clock at night, an avalanche of selling came in. I suggest that there must have been some leak in the information. The acting minister should make an investigation to see if such was the case, and if so, disciplinary action should be taken. It would be taken anywhere else.
^ Mr. G. H. CASTLEDEN (Yorkton): Speaking in opposition to this bill, because of the fact that it taxes cooperatives, removing, by the repeal of section 4(p), the protection previously enjoyed by cooperatives across Canada, I want to say first that I think this is a distinct departure from Liberal policy. Ever since 1930 cooperative organizations have enjoyed that protection. The legislation which provided it was placed there, I believe, because the government at that time recognized that true cooperatives are not profit making institutions; and by subjecting them to taxation the government is attacking the basic principles upon which cooperatives are bui'llt, and the Liberal party is ranging itself alongside those who have found that their privileged position, their rights to exploit the people, are being attacked by the growth of the cooperative movement in this country.
In 1,930 the cooperative movement had not become a very serious menace to monopolistic organizations. To-day, I think, cooperatives stand on the threshold of taking their proper place in the economy of the country. Wherever capitalism operates and controls an economy, big business comes to the fore and restricts supply, with the natural consequence that prices go up, profits increase, and the people who cannot afford to purchase have to go without. This is particularly true when the commodity they control is an absolute necessity, such as food, clothing, housing, medicine, health supplies, and, in the case of the farmer, machinery and oil and the other things he requires with which to make his living. Those who support the present system say, "Oh, competition will take care of that", but if you make a study of the situation you will find that the last thing that big business wants or will tolerate is competition. If a little fellow starts in 'business, big business will soon cut his throat, and any means that they can use will certainly go. The result has been that in self-protection the people have banded themselves into organizations which can carry on their business not to make profit for themselves but to supply their members with the services they require, about the only resource left to the common man to-day to protect himself against that exploitation is-
Politics.

-to get busy and form himself into cooperatives. The hon. member can talk about his gold; he is very well versed in that, I think, but let him leave this to me and make his speech about gold afterwards. My life has been spent out on the western
Income War Tax

prairies. Throughout the years I have seen the farmer bring his produce into the market to sell it. At one time he used to be able to sell his cattle and hogs privately to butchers, but now he sells them to the packers. At one time, too, he brought his loads of grain to the local elevators where he had the advantage of a certain amount of competition. But gradually the control of these elevators got into the hands of fewer and fewer companies, until finally there was only one market in which the farmer could sell his produce. The big boys got control, and could charge the farmer anything they liked for handling his grain. In those days, as I well remember, the farmer might come to town and go from one elevator to the other, only to find that they were all together on the price, and he had to take whatever price they told him. Their costs of taking in grain and loading it they kept to themselves, but they charged six cents or eight cents a bushel, or whatever they wanted to charge. The farmer found it impossible to break into that market alone, and at last a few of them said, "How about a bunch of us getting together and building a loading platform at the side of the railroad?" You remember the fight these people had years ago to get the right to build loading platforms where they could load their own grain on their own cars-a course to which they were forced because-the costs of handling were so tremendously high. Gradually out of these activities there grew the grain growers' organization and the wheat pools. To-day the farmers own their own elevators; they can set their own handling charges; they own their own output; they can sell their grain. Handling charges have gone down, and dockage can be better controlled. They have some say about the price; and the pool has gradually attained to a position where, as far as Saskatchewan is concerned, it handles fifty per cent of the grain grown in the province. To-day we see a fight between these cooperative organizations and the grain exchange monopolies which are opposed to the growth of these people's movements. But because of the growth of the pools the farmer has received a larger income, he has some control of his own economic destiny, he has acquired a certain measure of freedom, and the people resent very seriously anything which would curtail or destroy their opportunities to fight for their rights in a democratic way.
Some years ago I visited parts of Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, and talked with the lobster fishermen. They had had much the same experience. When they brought in their lobsters for sale they were told. "This is the price you are going to get." Gradually the

lobster fishermen got together, subscribed a little capital, and agreed to sell and handle their own products, with the result that the price return to them increased three or four hundred per cent. That is the story of cooperation:	where the people themselves
have taken hold they have been able to improve their means of livelihood and raise their standards of living. In my own province' the farmers built a big cooperative refinery because they objected to the prices the big boys were charging for oil. Now we see a two million dollar concern owned by the farmers and engaged in oil refining, and the price at which they are able to produce and sell to their customers and to themselves is a revelation to those who remember what they had to pay for their tractor gasoline in the days before the operation of that organization. More recently we have seen an effort made by the people to establish a factory wherein they can produce their own farm machinery and reveal the actual cost of production, since the selling price of this machinery seemed to bear no relation to the cost price, the costs of repairs and handling were exorbitant, competition was wiped out, and there was nothing they could do about it. Exactly the same principle operates when men have nothing to sell but tihe sweat of their brow. They cannot go individually and talk to the boss; they cannot sell to him, so they band together and form a union. What the cooperative is to the farmer the trade union is to the worker and the labouring man: it is a grouping together of the people to protect themselves and put up a fight for their rights as citizens to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
There are those who try to drive a wedge between labour and the farmer and who blame labour for everything that happens. But actually the people who produce the food and the people who produce the goods, the real wealth of the country, are in principle the same. It is interesting to note that the people who fight the cooperatives are the same people who fight and oppose the trade unions, democratically operated and democratically controlled. The unions and the cooperatives give men an opportunity to have some say in the running of their own affairs. They may make mistakes. That is quite natural, because they are only human. Nevertheless they represent the effort of the common people to advance themselves and overcome obstacles that appear almost insurmountable. After years of toil they have built up these organizations,

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was a point made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Castleden) on which I should like to say a few words. The suggestion was made that the Liberal party is aligning itself on the side of those who are in favour of big business, capitalism and so on, as opposed to the interests of the great masses of the people, and particularly the farmer. This bald statement was followed by the suggestion that some body formed the cooperatives without indicating in any way whatsoever just who was responsible for the formation of the cooperatives which have been spoken of during the last few moments.
There is some advantage in being young. Some of us realize that. But when one who is much younger speaks from memory perhaps he may be excused for his memory not being quite long enough. It is true that we have the largest cooperatives in the dominion operating in the province of Saskatchewan and handling more than fifty per cent of the grain produced in that province. But when my hon. friend gets up and tries to give credit to anyone other than the Liberal party for the establishment and development of the cooperatives, he is assuming something which history does not bear out.
On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You have made your speech. Let me make mine. It is nearly one o'clock.
On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I did not imply anything about the Liberal party. It was the people themselves that built up these cooperatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is no point of privilege in that. I will indicate who was responsible for the development.
Back in 1906 the first cooperative branch of any department of government in Canada, so far as I am aware, was established in Saskatchewan, and one has only to look at the record to know which government was in power at that time. The minister who established that branch to deal with cooperatives in the Department of Agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan afterwards became minister of agriculture in the federal government, but
while he was minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan he appointed Mr. Booth as the head of the cooperative organization in Saskatchewan. Mr. Booth was afterwards taken to Washington by the United States government to take part in the development of cooperatives there. Then when Mr. Motherwell became minister of agriculture at Ottawa he brought Mr. Booth back and placed him at the head of the agricultural economics division of the Department of Agriculture for the dominion to deal with cooperatives.
Back in the early days there were other advocates of state socialism besides those who now call themselves the C.C.F. party. The grain growers of Saskatchewan and Manitoba in 1908 advocated government ownership of elevators. The Conservative party in the province of Manitoba advocated government ownership of elevators. The Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan said that both the Conservative party and the farm organizations were wrong. They said that the proper way to meet the situation described by the member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden), presented by the big organization of elevator companies, was for the farmers themselves to organize their own cooperatives. That question was battled out on the floor of the grain growers' association as far back as 1908, 1909 and 1910, and in 1911 the Saskatchewan legislature passed an act establishing cooperative elevators. That was done by a Liberal government in Saskatchewan. It was not the farmers who advocated establishment of the cooperatives in Saskatchewan. It was the Liberal party, in battle with the farm organization.
Why do you try to kill them now?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, why do we try to kill them? We are not trying to kill them. The Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan at that time established those cooperatives. Those cooperatives were afterwards turned into what today is known as the pool elevator company. I myself was premier of Saskatchewan at the time this took place, and as my hon. friend knows, I went out into the province at the time and supported the organization of the pool. I not only did that, but opposed those previously connected with the old organization selling the shares of the farmers to their own advantage. As a result of that I met with considerable opposition from some of those who had been previously in that organization. All that is a matter of history.
In Saskatchewan to-day we have great cooperatives, not because anyone else took the initiative but because the Liberal party of

that day in Saskatchewan took the initiative and established the cooperatives there.
Now I come to the question of taxation. My hon. friend has said there was something done back in 1930. Who was here in 1930 when that was done?
Mr. Dunning.

Yes, and something was also done in the late thirties. Who was here at that time? Again Mr. Dunning. Mr. Dunning was a Liberal. He was a past premier of Saskatchewan, in which these cooperatives had been established. He was the first manager of the Cooperative Elevator company in Saskatchewan. The whole history of cooperatives is written around Liberalism and members of the Liberal party.
The suggestion is made that, there is something wrong with the present legislation. That goes back to the fact that a commission was established to inquire into the cooperatives, and one of the most important members of that commission was the deputy minister who is in charge of cooperatives in Saskatchewan to-day under the C.C.F. government there. The matters complained of by some members of the house were unanimously recommended by that commission. On some of the points raised here there was a unanimous report by the commission, which included the support of the gentleman who is deputy minister in charge of cooperatives in Saskatchewan now, and who I admit was trained under the Liberals during the time they were in power in Saskatchewan. But he was still retained by the C.C.F. government as one of the best informed and most active promoters of cooperatives in the Dominion of Canada. On that commission he recommended some of the very things that are being opposed by the members of the C.C.F. here to-day. The recommendations of that commission were taken largely as they were presented to the government, and presented to the house. But the house is not being asked to accept them holus-bolus as presented. Changes have been made as a result of the discussions that have taken place here and throughout the country.
All I wish to say now is that the whole record indicates that the real founders of the cooperative movement in the Dominion of Canada were the members of the Liberal party. Their policies have been behind the cooperative movement; they are still behind it, and when this legislation gets through it will have the support of the very people who my friends of the C.C.F. party are trying to lead us to believe are opposed to it in the province of Saskatchewan.
