Mr. Speaker, I recognize we are all anxious to further the business of the house and bring the session to an end as speedily as possible; nevertheless I feel it is important for me to follow up the remarks of the member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and the member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) in their protests against the provisions of the bill now before parliament for the taxation of cooperatives.
I do not believe that the government can feel ha.ppy about the sections of the bill providing for taxation of cooperatives, but however much we may censure it for having brought this legislation in, I want to express gratitude for the modifications of the original intentions as they were expressed in the budget resolutions. Still, these modifications are not enough.- The fact is that cooperatives are still being taxed.
Just before the house rose, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) endeavoured to persuade parliament that the cooperative movement in Canada had been built by the Liberal party. I do not feel like arguing that point at present, because there are other things more important to talk about, but I would say that perhaps no movement in the history of this country has been so free from any source of political partisanship as the cooperative movement. The cooperative movement, in Canada as in other countries, was born out of the economic necessity of the common people. It was an effort to supplement their meagre incomes or at least to extend them so that they could buy more goods. That was the primary moving force of the cooperative movement, and if the Liberal party can claim any credit for the building of the cooperatives in Canada it must be because that economic need which forced the common people to work together for ameliorative action was more intense under the Liberal government than -under any other. If that is the reasoning of the Minister of Agriculture, then of course there is no argument about it; we will allow him to go off with the prize in that connection. But if the Liberal party is the father of the cooperative movement, it is hard for us to understand why it should now wish to kill the child which so far is has nurtured. This legislation, harmless as it may appear to some, and almost insignificant in its understandable declaration, definitely points in the direction of the destruction of the cooperative movement.
I wish to register my objections to the sections of this bill which provide for the

Income War Tax
taxation of cooperatives, and I shall mention each particular feature and make a brief comment upon it.
I object to this measure in the first place because it does not define a cooperative, and, failing to define a cooperative, the legislation proceeds to twist the cooperative movement into the distinctive features of a capitalist and profit-seeking movement in order that it may be taxable. That is the actual situation as I see it; for the bill under discussion provides for the taxation of income and profits; since there are no profits in a cooperative it cannot be taxed, and if "cooperative" had been properly defined, that definition would have brought the cooperatives outside the bounds of the taxation scheme of the budget. This being the situation, no attempt is made to define cooperatives at all, but an attempt is made to compel cooperatives to adopt certain definite characteristics of a private profit-making institution in order to bring the movement within the ambit of the taxation scheme. That is the first thing I object to.
The second objection is that the twelve months within which all patronage devidends which have not been paid out to the customers will become taxable is not a great improvement on six months; for it is obvious that any cooperative might very well desire to have much longer use of its unpaid patronage dividends than that, and the necessity might be so great, in the development of the movement and even for the protection of the institution itself, that the use of such patronage dividends might be imperative. But if this legislation passes it will have to be paid out within the twelve months or else become taxable, and that is equivalent of course to taxing the capital of the organization and not income at all.
All the tax which may be imposed under this measure is in my view a tax on capital, because all the so-called income of cooperatives which may be taxable is composed of patronage dividends which in the first place have come out of the pockets of the people in wrhose name those patronage dividends stand and are therefore not taxable in the real sense of the word. But if they are left in and used in the operations of the business they become capital, and if they are left in for over twelve months they become taxable. Therefore this is taxation of capital and not taxation of profits of any cooperative.
I object to the measure also because, while it provides that new cooperatives shall not be taxed for three years, it makes no provision for cooperatives which may have been organized six months ago, one year ago, eighteen 63260-298
months ago or two years ago. They will be immediately taxable when this bill becomes law; therefore they do not get the three years, and the taxation of such small cooperatives might be crushing to them at this stage of their development.
I object to the retaining or the compulsion to retain an amount equal to three per cent of the working capital. This is the basis of the taxation scheme. This is the principle by which cooperatives are compelled to assume the characteristics of an ordinary private enterprise seeking profit as an objective. This is the means by which cooperatives are being forced to assume the characteristics of a capitalist institution in order that the government may be justified in imposing taxes upon them. These are the main points which I and my associates object to in this legislation.
I should like to say that I appreciate the fact that the government has been under tremendous pressure from the private interests of the country which feel that they cannot do business as economically arid give the same service to the public as the cooperatives. They are not prepared to meet the competition of cooperatives. They feel that if cooperation keeps on developing and becomes federated to carry on the business of the people on a nonprofit basis, ultimately it will be a decided challenge to some of the greatest industries or the greatest businesses of Canada. That is a possibility. The private interests have seen that possibility, and perhaps never before has there been so extensive and expensive campaigning to influence the government and parliament to interfere with the development of cooperatives and to lay hands upon it in such a way as to retard its growth. I have never seen such a campaign in my memory.
I understand that the government has been under great pressure, and as I said at the beginning, I feel that the government is not happy about the legislation. It has tried to tax cooperatives without taxing them; it has tried to please the other side by imposing taxation on cooperatives, and therefore there is a dilemma. In the last analysis it has turned out that the government apparently could not draw all the sections without some teeth in them, and there are teeth in them. Such teeth as are there will tend to bite off the head of the cooperatives. If it is not enough this year, they will add a little more next year, and the year following a little more still, until eventually they will limit the operation of the cooperatives and ultimately destroy the movement.
Therefore I would appeal first of all to the hon. gentleman who claims that his party is the father of the cooperative movement in

Mr. Speaker I just wish to say that the members of this group are opposed to the principle of the bill because we regard the underlying principle as being that governments must be dependent upon taxation for their revenue. We have always maintained that the real purpose of taxation should be to remove redundant purchasing power from circulation -that is, that portion of the purchasing power of the people which may create an effective demand against production in excess of the ability of industry to satisfy it. Furthermore, we feel that the purpose of taxation should be to bring about a fairer distribution of the production of the country until such time as production has expanded to meet the needs of the people. To the extent that that type of taxation fails to meet government expenditures, we believe that the government should use national money. Until we do that, we can take it for granted that in the future the national debt will continue to expand as it has in the past, and also that our debt charges will expand, thereby requiring an increase in taxation to meet them, resulting of course in still greater discontent amongst the workers of the country, thereby bringing about a reduction in or a retarding of production.
Hon. members on the government side and in other parts of the house are continually warning of the danger of socialism, communism and every other form of "ism." But I should like to point out that so long as the government continues in the future as they have in the past to use a deflationary policy we are breeding a condition that brings about communism and socialism.
I should also like to suggest to the government that they might very well take heed of the suggestion of the national resources plan-

ning board of the United States. I quote from page 105 of a book entitled "Where's the Money Coming From?" by Mr. Stuart Chase, who has this to say:
If the government borrowed solely from its own central bank without interest, there need be no interest burden at all. There would be amortization of the principal, and the fundamental prohibition not to pump too many new dollars into the system would still stand.' The national resources planning board has said: "Should the day arrive when the carrying charge on the federal debt becomes oppressive, serious thought should be given to the creation by our modern banking and treasury institutions of non-interest-bearing debt.
I hope the government will not wait until the situation becomes so chronic that our production will have already started to fall and unemployment will have started to increase. The war is over, and no longer is it necessary for fifty per cent of our production to go for the purposes of war. Therefore it is only natural that the people of the country should have expected to find in the budget a substantial reduction in income tax of people in the low income brackets. I should like to place before this house the definite stand of this group in regard to cooperatives. Our definite stand is that there should be no taxation on cooperatives except on patronage dividends of non-members that are not distributed; and provided that patronage dividends are only withheld by cooperatives with the consent of their members. I cannot see any possible justification for the provision in this bill which places a tax upon an amount of capital equivalent to three per cent. I am not going to deal further with that point now; I shall wait until the bill reaches the committee stage.
This morning several hon. members commented upon the need for expansion of production by the gold mines of this country. During the war the members of this group consistently attacked the production of gold in war time, because we felt that production of that sort was bound to impede our war effort. We needed production elsewhere, and we required all the labour and all the materials that could be made available. Therefore we felt that using labour and materials for the production of gold was not helping the war effort at all. To-day of course the situation is somewhat different, but nevertheless throughout the world there is a great shortage of food, clothing, and housing, and I fail to see how the production of gold can help in any shape or form to alleviate that sort of want. However. I would agree that so long as other nations are willing and perhaps anxious to give us $35 worth of goods for an ounce of gold there is a good argument for continuing the production of gold; but on the other hand I do not think there is any justification whatsoever for subsidizing the production of gold for export by low grade ore mines, any more than there would be justification for subsidizing other kinds of production that was uneconomic. As long as our labour and capital can be utilized for production that will bring more wealth to the country, low grade mines should not be subsidized.
I am not going to say more at this stage, but we shall have a few words to say on various sections of the bill when we get into committee.

Belief in gold is deep rooted in human nature, and has been for many centuries. It is not going to disappear overnight. I think everyone in the house will agree that in the last few years the gold industry has been, you might almost say, a cornerstone of our economy, and has come to the assistance of that economy in times when it was very greatly in need of that assistance.
The next point I want to make is that I think we will all agree, as I believe the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) himself agreed when he made the statement, that the change to parity did in fact greatly embarrass the gold industry. I am not going to make any comment on that, other than to indicate the fact, on which every one agrees; and the best proof of that lies in the action of the government itself coming along and endeavouring to give assistance to the industry so that it could continue to provide employment, continue to bring to this country valuable goods and services in return for the export of the gold. As I say, the government came forward with this measure. I think there will be wide agreement that it was a wise step to take; but the question which now arises and which I think is in the minds of everyone is whether or not that relief was well conceived. When I heard the figures read in this house by the Acting Minister of Finance I was not sufficiently familiar with the situation to appreciate whether or not the assistance was practical; but as I listened this morning to the figures given by the hon. member for York West, prepared by the Ontario Mining association, if I remember aright, a serious body, figures which have not been questioned in any way, they seemed to me in the highest degree trivial. I thought the hon. member was fully warranted in asking whether or not they indicated a really serious desire on the part of the government to assist the industry. The hon. member for York West said it was a gesture. Well, Mr. Speaker

it seems to me I would be well within the limits of the truth in saying that if it was a gesture it was not even a polite gesture; and I am sure if I attempted to illustrate the kind of gesture I think it really was you would rebuke me sharply and say I was insulting the dignity and decorum of this house.
Finally, it seemed to me the hon. member for York West did indicate a reasonable, practical and proved method of increasing this assistance, and I see no reason why assistance on the lines he recommended would not be reasonable. I realized it more than ever the other day, when I heard a man from the north country, a man who I think knew fully what he was talking about, remark to another man in the mining industry that if things continue as they are now that northern, mining country, which depends on gold, will be a desert within ten years. I am not asking the house to accept that statement. Predictions are often made which are exaggerated, and1 there may be other adjustments that can be made under which the industry will be able to continue. Nevertheless I think there is a measure of agreement on this, that it is an important matter, and the government has given an indication that it regards it as an important matter by actually proffering a measure of assistance, though if the figures which have been given are corect, and they have not been challenged, that assistance is of a trivial nature. So I am suggesting to the minister that the government might very well review its decision to see whether, instead of this trivial gesture, it cannot come forward with a really substantial measure of help.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that the effect of reenacting this section, which is as it now stands in the law, will not be to exempt from taxation the additional $2,000 paid to members of the senate in virtue of the legislation passed last year. Will the indemnities of members of the legislative council of Quebec be exempt from taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend will notice that the word is "elected", an elected member of a provincial legislature. They will not be exempt.
Is this section based on resolution No. 27?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: ' It is based on several resolutions.
Was there not in the resolution an alternative that a person who left employment and received a lump sum could have that lump sum taxed at the rate of taxation for the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct. There are several sections in the bill which relate to that resolution covering lump sum payments. So that in some subsequent section I shall find that part of the resolution which provided that a man receiving money could elect to be taxed at the rate of taxation of the last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend is correct.

With reference to subsection 6 of section 3 being repealed and the following being substituted therefor:
"Where the minister is satisfied that a single payment" and so on, and again with reference to subsection 8 of section 3, am I correct in saying that there can be no reversal by the appeal board of any decision made by the minister to whom the application is made under these sections? If I am correct in that, and I think I am, having regard to section 69(e) I wish to raise this point. One of the recommendations of the senate committee was that decisions made by the minister, in other words discretionary decisions, should be subject to appeal. I am going to deal with that when I come to the section in question. I feel that even at this stage some mention should be made of the power that rests in the minister under a provision such as this. I will not refer to the evidence that was taken or to the recommendations of the senate, but this and other sections run counter to the recommendation of the senate committee, which was that there should be a board of taxation appeals with power to review all matters of assessment and all matters of fact and of law. The evidence taken before that committee was representative of more than twenty organizations across the country, and there was no objection. I know that in my own province of Saskatchewan farmers are approached by inspectors. The farmers have not kept books, and an arbitrary fixation is made against which they have no appeal-a decision of some office holder, made without regard to law or fact. When this matter was before the senate committee there was only one person who objected, and that was Mr. Fraser Elliott, who said that there should be no appeal on discretionary matters. In the senate report the statement is made that Mr. Elliott made a recommendation that there be no appeal, and that was contrary to every other recommendation that had been made.
In my opinion the granting of discretionary powers to the minister, and allowing him to determine, without regard to law or fact, but relying on his own conception of justice, what persons shall come within the purview of subsection 6 of section 3 or subsection 8 of section 3, is a dangerous principle for parliament to reenact. I should like to hear from the minister what justification there is for taking away from the courts or from the board of appeals the right to decide this matter on the law and the facts, on appeal from a decision made by some office holder or the discretionary order of the minister, which after all is the order of the officials. This is just one more example of a trend which is greatly accelerating. After all, the senate is an integral part of parliament, representing all parts of Canada. They heard the evidence of many groups across
Income War Tax

the country and decided to recommend a certain course of action. That course was not followed because of the fact that what can almost be said to be a hierarchy of civil servants outside are able to determine what is good for the people, regardless of the views of parliament.
Some may say that that is not the position. While I may not refer to another debate of the present session, I may say that when veterans affairs were under discussion, as is reported at page 4483 of Hansard of August 8, the parliamentary assistant to the minister, explaining why the unanimous recommendation of the committee on veterans affairs had not been followed, said that two officials of his department thought that they knew more than a committee of parliament, and the government followed the recommendation of the two civil servants rather than the unanimous recommendation of the committee.
Shocking.

At this stage I should like to hear from the minister what is the view of the government with regard to the recommendation that there should be a right of appeal in respect of ministerial decisions. Why is this great power still to be vested in the minister, subject to no appeal even to the board of tax appeals? After all, while on the face of it the right of appeal is being granted, it means very little, because approximately eighty per cent of all the decisions made by the income tax department will be and are construed as discretionary matters. Fearing that someone may consider that in taking this view I am partisan I need only refer the minister to an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of August 9, where the whole question of discretionary powers is reviewed under the heading "Discretion Unlimited." The editorial goes on to say:
After the approval of its budget in parliament the Canadian government presumably will proceed without delay to set up two new faxing boards which are designed to assure a larger measure of justice for the taxpayer. These boards should improve our existing taxation system but. on analysis, their powers fall far short of what our taxpayer deserves. Though they are based on the recent studies of a senate committee they fail to carry out the committee's report at its most vital point.
Then further on:
The most important principle of the senate report-the power of the appeal board to consider how tax officials use their discretion and to revoke their discretionary decisions-is thus destroyed by the government's plan.
No matter what the walk of life may be, taxpayers in every section of this dominion have found themselves subject to orders based on the discretionary principle and denied the

right of appeal. I suggest to the minister that if we are to remake the War Income Tax Act, which apparently is the intention, having regard to the number of amendments that are brought down, something more than a brief explanation is due to the committee as to why these discretionary powers are to be perpetuated. In excepting some twenty per cent of the cases, the decision of office holders in the civil service or of the minister by way of final appeal in all discretionary matters will still continue to be supreme.
I would ask the minister to make a statement in the matter, because it is one which deserves the serious attention of the committee and is of interest to people all over the country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to do that. I had assumed that we should have a considerable discussion on the matter of the exercise of discretionary powers when we were dealing with the sections relating to the appellate board and the advisory board. I really think it might be more convenient to the committee if we did it then.
As my hon. friend appreciates as well as or better than most other hon. members of the committee, these numerous discretionary powers fall under various heads. Some are the exercise of powers with respect to the refusal to grant exemptions or allowances, as was pointed out in the senate committee report. Others involve administrative or punitive powers. Some involve constituting the minister a judge of reasonableness or equity, and so on. When we reach these sections I shall be prepared to discuss the various categories in some detail and give the reasons why it was felt that most of these discretions should be reviewed by the advisory board rather than the appeal board.
As my hon. friend appreciates, this section is in effect the reenactment of an existing section with the following words added: "between the first day of January and the 27th day of June." The discretion which is contained in this section is not a new one conferred by this amending bill. The subsection is the reenacting of an existing one with the addition of certain words. Therefore unless my hon. friend insists, I should prefer to deal with them when we are dealing with the sections relating to the appeal board and the advisory board.

I bring it up now because all the way along until we get to section 69 we shall be enacting discretionary powers. Finally when we come to section 69 we shall have established all these matters,

Income War Tax
and then we shall discuss the why and the wherefore.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: So far as I know we are not establishing by this bill many new discretionary powers. We are reenacting sections. There may be one or two which are necessary, but I think I am safe in saying there are not many more than that. The new powers which we would have to consider are the ones which have been in .the act or added to the act over a period of years. I should prefer to discuss them when we are discussing the details of these provisions.

Is the minister willing to add a clause to the effect that the discretion of the minister is appealable? As I understand it, in the past the discretion has been a little broader, and the exchequer court has refused to interfere with it. We are setting up two appellate divisions, and if there were an appeal from the minister's discretion I think we would all be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am sure some people would be satisfied, but that strikes at the principle of ministerial discretion and responsibility. In Great Britain, where the same principle of conferring ministerial discretion is followed, there is an appeal to the courts, but the courts have always dealt with it in this way, that if the discretion, as I have said several times before in the house, has been exercised in a bona fide way they do not review the exercise of that discretion.. In its very nature it implies the exercise of judgment on the part of someone; that is what discretion means. It is an opinion. I shall discuss some of these reasons a little more fully when we get to the advisory board sections, but my hon. friend's suggestion strikes at the very root of the granting of ministerial discretion. It is easy to .talk in broad general terms about the undesirability of conferring discretionary powers under an act of this kind, but I say to this committee that from a practical point of view it is impossible to draft a workable income tax aOt of this kind without putting in such discretions, and that it is impracticable to give an appeal to the courts from the exercise of such discretion. That responsibility must be assumed by the minister of the crown upon whom parliament confers it, and for the life of me I do not see how we could properly ask the courts to review a discretion properly exercised by a responsible minister of the crown. It is all very well to say that it is exercised by bureaucrats and civil servants and so on, but the final responsibility is upon the minister, and under the new procedure we are providing under this act there is a very real opportunity for review and consideration
by the minister himself. However, I shall discuss that when we come to the section in question.

The minister has made the categorical statement that it would be impracticable to give an appeal on discretionary matters. He said there was an appeal to the exchequer court in the event that the discretion had not really been exercised, or had not been exercised honestly or fairly, or that the person exercising the discretion was influenced by extraneous and irrelevant facts; that is the law to-day. Hemmed in by those considerations, there is really no appeal; but my hon. friend makes the categorical statement that an appeal on questions of judgment, as he says, or discretion, would! be impracticable.
Let me tell my hon. friend that before this senate committee, composed of outstanding members of that body, appeared, representatives of the Canadian federation of agriculture, the trades and labour congress of Canada, life insurance companies, the income tax payers' association, the Canadian federation of labour, the Edmonton and Regina chambers of commerce, the dominion association of chartered accountants, the Canadian bar association, stock exchanges, the Toronto board of trade, the Canadian electrical association, the Federation Canadienne et Catholique du Travail-[DOT]and the Montreal chamber of commerce. All these bodies, representative of agriculture and business, came before this committee and were ail of the opinion that an appeal was proper. The only one who took the opposite view was Mr. Elliott. The report of the special committee states:
Mr. Elliott indicated, however, that the findings of the board or committee should in essence be advisory only and that should the Minister of National Revenue desire to adhere to a conclusion differing with the findings of the board, no further review or appeal should be provided but that, as is the case under the presently enacted legislation, the decision of the minister in respect thereto should be final and conclusive.
That is the same argument made by the minister to-day, but this is w-hat the committee of the senate unanimously report:
Your committee has given consideration to these submissions of the deputy minister and has concluded that they represent a direct conflict of opinion with the suggestion advanced brother witnesses in briefs and examinations, with which suggestions your committee agrees in principle as will be hereafter shown.
I point out that while the minister gives a categorical answer that the right of appeal from a decision of the minister on matters of discretion is impracticable except within the limited purview of the authorities, one of the most recent of which is Nicholson v Minister

mi

of National Revenue, on the other hand practically all business organizations and bodies representing agriculture in this country stated that it was practicable, and that there should be a right of appeal. While I accept the minister's suggestion that further discussion take place later, I do want to point out that while he takes one view, the only person supporting that view is Mr. Elliott, and against that view is the view of all these other organizations representing all the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for deferring further discussion until we reach the sections dealing with the tax boards. I point out, of course, that these various organizations he listed made other submissions to the senate committee than those relating to these discretionary powers. I read a good many of their briefs, which I remember covered many points; in fact- some did not make much reference to discretionary powers. However, I think the issues at this preliminary stage have been made fairly clear as between the view put forward by my, hon. friend and the view I have voiced, and perhaps that should suffice for the question of principle when we consider the various discretionary powers in the subsequent sections.
Section 2 agreed! to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The suggestion has
been made that section 3 should be considered paragraph by paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I believe that would be wise. I think it would1 make for more orderly discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then I shall call section 3.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I have an amendment here which I am going to ask one of my colleagues to move, but it relates to paragraph (3), so I shall take it up when we come to that paragraph.
On section 3, subsection 1-Mutual corporation.

I should like to make a few remarks on this section, as it affects a good many cash mutual companies in my part of the country, North Waterloo, Perth and South Waterloo. These cash mutuals, as I interpret this section of the act, are very adversely affected. In the past they have been paying three per cent tax on premiums, and now are also to be taxed on income. Originally the companies I refer to carried on the fire insurance business only, but while the bulk of their business continues to be fire
fMr. Diefenbaker.]
insurance, some of the companies write auto- [DOT] mobile and casualty lines. A large proportion of their business is in Ontario, Quebec and the western provinces.
The cash mutuals began as premium note mutuals insuring farms, village and local risks in southwestern Ontario in the same manner as the many farm mutuals which have served the farming community in the absence, until recently and now only to a limited extent, of any general farm insurance service from the stock companies. It is estimated that over $500,000,000 in farm fire insurance in Ontario, aside from Quebec, which is over eighty per cent of the total, is carried in mutual companies such as the ones I have described, and that over 197,000 Ontario farmers are insured in mutuals. The cash mutuals insure at least 16,000 farm risks, as well as a large number of village, town and other risks which are not protected by municipal or other fire fighting organizations. Many of the stock companies will not insure these unprotected risks, and if they do they are usually at higher rates.
The cash mutuals operate on a cash premium system as well as on the premium note basis. This development of the cash premium is a departure from the original scheme, which relied on the premium note for the large part of the policyholder's premium. Mutuals always demanded some payment in advance, as was required under the terms of the earliest legislation. It has been required in legislation since. As early as 1868 the legislature recognized the need of permitting business on a cash-mutual basis and authorized assessments for purposes of establishing reserves.
This brings me to my point, that under the new plan, as I understand it-and probably the minister will clear up this point-the premiums are taxed and the profits are taxed. No one objects to paying taxes, because what is fair for one is fair for another. But in cases such as this, where double taxation is now proposed, it places in a very unfavourable position these companies whose policy in the past has been to create reserves to protect the insured. Either one tax or the other should be eliminated.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am aware of the situation my hon. friend has outlined with respect to mutual insurance companies. As he knows, they were dealt with by the McDougall report, and the proposed section in large measure implements the recommendations contained in that report. It is true that up to the present time mutual insurance companies have been completely exempt from any form of income tax. The McDougall commission

Income War Tax
recommended that that should not continue. The principal tax on the mutual insurance companies is the premium tax, to which my hon. friend made reference. Under the Special War Revenue Act, which was passed yesterday, the rate has been reduced from three per cent to two per cent for the deposit premium mutuals.
It is true that for the future mutual insurance companies will not be permitted to build up reserves out of undistributed taxable income. But any refunds which they make to policyholders, which are the equivalent of patronage dividends by cooperatives, are deductible from the gross income for purposes of taxation. So that I do not feel the new provision will be a serious interference with the operations of the mutual insurance companies. They will in fact be on exactly the same basis as the cooperatives, and on the basis recommended by the McDougall commission.

I spoke on this matter when we were discussing the resolutions, and since that time I have been able to obtain certain figures, which are too lengthy to place on Hansard. There are sixty-seven small farmers' mutuals in Ontario. I believe there are only one or two of them with reserves of more than $100,000. Many of them have reserves of $10,000, $15,000, or $16,000. I have been told by so many people that I believe it is true, without looking it up, that the Ontario government has insisted these mutuals have a reserve equal to two per cent of their insurance in force. It would seem that the smaller companies have from $8 million to $10 million of insurance in force, and therefore eventually they must build up to a reserve of around $100,000. That would apply to even the smallest of them.
This mutual fire insurance business is entirely different from the business of the cooperatives. A cooperative is an organization which buys something and sells it. At the end of the year it has certain moneys on hand which can be distributed as patronage dividends, if so desired. But the mutual fire insurance companies, which are operating in a comparatively small area and are able to protect themselves only by re-insurance, must build up good reserves. I have picked at random a small company operating in West Middlesex, the Caradoc mutual, which had losses in a particular year which left them no profits, or at least profits which were less than $1,000. But in nearly every case they have to build up reserves for bad years. Let us suppose that they build up $4,000 or $5,000
of profits in one year. As I understand it, they will come under the corporation tax of 30 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think that is correct. In common with other organizations they cannot build up reserves out of taxable income. They can build up reserves up after the tax has been paid.

But everything is not the same. I am speaking about the small farmers' mutuals. I say these farmers' mutual fire insurance companies are different from cooperatives. There is no use in saying they are the same. There are always exceptions; indeed if there were no exceptions there would not be the discretion vested in the minister, to which we are objecting, and the possibility that a different discretion would be exercised in respect of some other organization.
Let me follow this through to its logical conclusion. I have in mind a small farmers' mutual which may have an income in one year of $10,000. I am thinking of many of them in that position. Perhaps they will pay out for management and losses the sum of $7,000, and they would have only $3,000 left to meet any future losses. The government will take $900 of that. Perhaps next year that company will have many losses and no income. I do not suppose the government will come along and give the $900 back to them. I suggest we should understand fully the work that these farmers' mutuals do. It is entirely different from buying and selling. They must protect one another against large losses which may be suffered by their members, and in that way give reimbursement which arises from that unfortunate position. They are doing the work that larger companies do not want. I am not in the insurance business, but I know enough about insurance to know that the large companies do not want to insure isolated farm houses or bams, because they have no fire protection. No one is near them. They are bound to suffer loss. Some of the insurance these mutuals carry would be in the form of risks in connection with lightning striking farm animals. I was astonished when I learned the amount of damage done to horses and cattle by lightning.
And wind damage, too.
Yes, there is also weather damage. It would be a tremendous tax, and one which we could very well do without.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I agree that farm mutuals do perform a service and have a type of insurance which most of the stock and other companies are not anxious to take. But there
Income War Tax

is no real difference in principle or practice between the service they are rendering to their members and that found in a cooperative organization. I do not agree with the hon. member when he says that the tax here is a serious matter. The heavy and the important tax in connection with all these mutuals is the premium tax; there is no doubt about that. If these mutuals have already built up a reserve, then of course it is there, and that is all there is to it.
Mr/ GRAYDON: There to-day but gone to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: But that is true of any other capital. No other group or organization can replace its capital out of current earnings, if it is lost, except out of earnings after tax. I should have pointed out that their losses are carried forward. They have all the privileges that other taxpayers have.

I did not realize that these mutual companies had the opportunity of distribution over several years. Have they? If they have a fortunate year, where they have no loss in ordinary income they will pay the tax on the large amount of surplus, and the next year if they have a heavy loss they will pay nothing, because they will not be in a position to pay anything.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The hon. member will recall that under the act passed a year ago losses can be carried one year back and three years forward.
For mutual companies?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: For any companies, any businesses.

The minister has said that this was recommended by the McDougall commission. In the recommendations at page 65 of the report we find this:
We are of the opinion that mutuals can and do have income which is subject to tax. This income results from investments and operating pains which are free from claims of policyholders. At the same time we consider that mutuals in certain specialized fields are rendering a service which is not provided by other organizations, notably, in insuring farm and other unprotected rural risks. These mutuals tend to keep their rates as low as is consistent with the risk involved. We consider that it would not be in the public interest to impose income tax upon those insurers whose activities are primarily in these fields.
Considering the situation as a whole, we are of the opinion that the income tax should not be imposed on mutuals 'without a review of the varying rates of existing premium tax under the Special War Revenue Act.
Then in the summary of recommendations, under section 5:

That the income of any insurer, mutual or otherwise, shall not be liable to taxation when in any year the net premium income in Canada is derived, to the extent of not less than 50 per cent thereof, from the insurance of farm property and other property not protected by municipal or other fire fighting organizations.
As the president of a mutual insurance company in my own riding, I would ask the minister to explain that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I said a moment ago that the legislation was largely implementing the provisions of the McDougall commission report. It is quite true, as my hon. friend points out, that in the case of mutual insurance companies doing more than fifty per cent of their business on farm property on the conditions mentioned, it was recommended that they should be exempted. That recommendation was considered by the minister and officials of this department, and it was felt that it was not desirable to set up a special class of mutual insurance company which would be completely exempt from tax. That is the reason why it was not felt that that particular recommendation could be implemented. Perhaps I should have pointed out that this class of mutual does enjoy complete exemption from payment of the premium tax if more than fifty per cent of their business is derived from insurance of farm property. I pointed that out in answer to the hon. member for Haldimand the other day. They have now a special exemption from premium tax.

If I may be permitted' to cite my own case, we have an insurance company with $5,000,000 worth of insurance policies. We are running at the rate of twenty cents per S100, from which we derive premiums of some $10,000. Our losses last year were $6,000; our expenses were $2,000, or a total of $8,000. Our earned surplus would then be around $2,000. Is the tax on that surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; there would be $60 tax there if it is not distributed. Of course, if it is distributed to policy holders, there would' be no tax.
Since we are compelled by the provincial act to keep a surplus we have $45,000 of a surplus on hand, and we are required to keep that up to a certain limit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If you have the $45,000, and it did not need the $2,000 that my hon. friend has mentioned in order to hold the $45,000 at $45,000, it could be turned back to the policy holders and, of course, would not be subject to tax.

As refund of premiums?'

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As refund of premiums, and then it is deductible and would not be subject to tax. I think the mutuals will find in practice that there is very little, if any, tax involved to them in this provision.
I think there is a tendency for the farm mutuals to lower their rate to get away from the income tax and then place themselves in a hazardous position if they incur a heavy loss.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They must exercise proper business judgment. Their managers and directors must follow the principles of ordinary business prudence,

I suppose that all of us from rural sections are interested in farm mutual insurance. I know that our own buildings years ago were insured in two different mutual companies; and on one occasion, some twenty or twenty-five years ago, the premium note with one company, which always forms part of the policy agreement, had to be paid in part by all those who had a policy with that particular mutual insurance company. I hope the minister is not forgetting that this is in an entirely different position from the ordinary premium paid to the ordinary insurance company, because, once you pay your premium to the ordinary commercial company, tariff or non-tariff, that is the end of it; but when you pay your premium to a mutual that is not necessarily the end of it, because, if a big storm comes, inflicting a tremendous amount of damage, be it by fire or whatever other cause, if that damage is concentrated in one particular area every farmer who is insured knows that he may
have to put up some part or all of the premium note which he has signed at the time he took the policy. That seems to me to put the mutual companies in a very different position from that of the others. When the hon. member for Perth speaks of $2,000 being left as a surplus on one year's business, to my mind that is the type of thing which shows good management and a desire to provide against loss in the future, and, more than that, to alleviate the possibility of some farmers having to put up money on the premium note in the future. This matter of the premium note, which is a liability existing on paper against every farmer holding a policy in a mutual company-at least, in the one we deal with-indicates an important and complete distinction affecting the question of taxation of these mutual companies. It may be that the minister is right when he says that not a great deal of taxation is likely to be levied against the company. But I think that if the principle is bad for $100 it is bad for $1,000 and it is bad for $100,000. I think the principle is an important one, and I should like the minister to reconsider this matter and see to it that these mutual companies do not have to pay this tax. I do not think it is a fair tax; it is one for which the farmers are going to have to foot the bill, and I think the farmers have already footed about enough bills in all the agricultural communities that I know of.

Before the minister replies, may I make one observation? Under the old act, by paragraph (g) the mutuals were exempted. We now have this section, which I must say I find difficulty in reading because there are two negatives, and I agree with the hon. member who said he found the drafting anything but clear, although it may have been difficult to do it in any other way. But what we find now is that the only mutuals that will get exemptions are those which deal wholly, apparently, with charitable institutions ; but you go on and still have the exemption as it was on life insurance companies except such as is credited to shareholders! account. The point I want to make is one with regard to which, it seemed to me, the minister gave a very by-and-large interpretation of the McDougall report, because in reading the section it seemed to me that the McDougall report goes completely in the face of what is now being done. "We consider", they say "it would not be in the public interest to impose income tax upon those insurers whose activities are primarily in these fields."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
What section is my hon. friend reading?
Income War Tax

I am reading now from page 65 of the report. I suggest that in changing the act you have made it worse than it was before, and in so doing, have gone flatly in the face of the recommendations of the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The McDougall commission reported that these mutuals should be put on the same basis as other cooperatives. They did suggest, in the case of farm mutuals more than fifty per cent of whose business was insuring farm property, exemption from taxation. The commission says on page 65:
We are of the opinion that mutuals can and do have income which is subject to tax. This income results from investments and operating gains which are free from claims of policy holders. At the same time we consider that mutuals in certain specialized fields are rendering a service which is not provided by other organizations, notably, in insuring farm and other unprotected rural risks. These mutuals tend to keep their rates as low as is consistent wuth the risk involved. We consider that it would not be in the public interest to impose income tax upon those insurers whose activities are primarily in these fields.
They recommended that if more than fifty per cent of the business was in insuring farm property they should be exempt. That was considered by the minister and his advisers, and it was felt that we should not single out a special class of insurance company for complete exemption. This particular class already receives special treatment by exemption from the premium tax, which is the important tax in this field. That is the tax on the fellow who pays the insurance premiums, for in the final analysis that is where -the tax has to go.
The hon. member for Peel said that there should not be any difference between $1,000 and $1,000,000.
I said the principle was the same.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I turn his statement around and say that the principle is exactly the same whether it is small or big. That was the reasoning which prompted the decision to treat all mutual corporations as being the same type of enterprise, but giving special consideration to the farm mutuals in connection with the premium tax which is imposed under the Special War Revenue Act.

I suggest that when you exempt the income of life insurance companies except such amount as is credited to shareholders' account you are in effect exempting life insurance business to the extent that the mutual feature is present in their enterprise, and therefore an inconsistency arises there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes, but my hon. friend knows that the principles which govern life

insurance underwriting are completely different from those which govern the underwriting of property and that the portion of the premium which goes into life insurance represents the savings of the people less certain amounts for the actuarial- risks involved. That has been in the act for years and I think is sound. But the mutual fire insurance companys are providing a community service through cooperative effort. They are not accumulating savings or buying protection against death. They are operating a mutual organization for mutual protection against certain risks, and average the costs of these risks. The principles which underlie that type of risk are completely different from those underlying life insurance. The principle which has been adopted in connection with the life insurance companies is that the shareholders' portion is, of course, taxed; the other part is not. Again, in the case of the life insurance companies there is a premium -tax.
The worst feature is that these companies can avoid taxation simply by sending cheques back at the end of the year to the people who are insured.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: So can any other cooperative.

That is starting them on the downward path of trying to evade taxation, which should be fixed and fair. Cheques will be sent back at the end of the year to the policy holders in order to avoid taxation. So that the government will not be any further ahead and a great deal of bother will be given to these mutual companies. That will be the only result.

We have in our province the Prince Edward Island Mutual Fire Insurance Company. It does business only with farm property. Ninety-five per cent of its insurance business is with farmers, the remainder with schools and churches. As I understand the McDougall report, a company of that kind would be exempt because practically all its premiums come from farm insurance. Is that type of company exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is what the McDougall report recommended.
And that is what is in the act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, that is not what is in the act.

That is what we want in the act. This is purely a farmers' mutual insurance company. It differs from most mutuals in that it has just a set rate. The farmers do not sign a note when they pay a premium for any liability that may occur. The company carries

the entire risk, and the premium is very small, about one-third of what the tariff premium is.
In this case-and there may be similar companies in the other provinces-I think the McDougall recommendation must apply. Surely the minister will make it apply in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know whether the company refunds premiums to its policy holders at the end of the year? I presume it does.
