speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The committee may recall that when we were discussing the resolution I indicated that I would give sympathetic consideration to the suggestions put forward that the section we are now considering should be made to apply not only to new cooperatives which started off without any previously acquired assets but to cooperatives which acquired an existing business. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech had indicated that it was the intention to restrict the operation of the section to a newly formed cooperative which had not acquired an . already existing business. That was prompted by the fear that the provision might be utilized to operate what was really a private business under the cloak of a cooperative organization. But after the matter was considered it was felt that provisions could be inserted in the law to guard against that, and that has been done. Hon. members will see that there is a provision that there must be at least twenty members in the cooperative and that each member must have an equal share. Members will see that paragraph (vii) provides that the business must not be a continuation of a previous business in which, in the opinion of the minister, a substantial number of members of the corporation had
a substantial interest, either as shareholders of a corporation carrying on the previous business or otherwise. So that with these protective clauses it is felt that the contingency of fraud is guarded against, and therefore the section is of general application to both a brand new business and one already existing.

I appreciate what the minister has said, and I am glad that, on appropriate advice, he has made these changes, which are important. There is, however, one other change which he has not yet seen the need of. I honestly believe that the minister wishes to do the right thing as far as possible, and I have not said any harsh things in this connection; but if he could see the point which I shall endeavour to make, I believe he would be willing to make the necessary changes. What I have to say comes under paragraph (p). That is the provision to which I wish particularly to speak. I have advised the minister why we feel it is necessary to strike out the date line there so as to allow this to apply to a cooperative that may have started in the last two years or two years and eleven months.
Let me give one illustration that will have application to many other situations. When I spoke before, I used this illustration in connection with the cooperative horse-marketing association. It may be funny to talk about horse meat here, but I can assure the committee that it is not funny to those people who eat horse meat, nor is it by any means funny to those who own horses that are running at large, consuming grass that should be eaten by cattle and sheep at a time when we need such meat. I am going to tell a brief story and if I leave the track, Mr. Chairman, or if you think I am leaving the track, I will come back to it at once. I can assure you I will not be riding horseback or bullback while telling this story.
The minister, I am sure, wishes to remedy the situation that exists at the moment, because he told us frankly one day that the country was not being run by experts, and I was glad to hear that, because experts make expert mistakes. Experts make expert mistakes, whereas simple people make simple mistakes that require only simple correction in order to bring matters back to where they were before. It is for that reason I am telling this story.
For many years, as hon. members no doubt know, horses were our main source of power, and therefore the raising of horses was a business indulged in by a great many people and to a large extent by those who had ranges which could accommodate horses. Id the last
Income War Tax

number of years, and particularly in the period of the depression, when costs of production had to be lowered, and during the war years when man-power was at a premium and machine power had to be introduced, it developed that horse owners, large anl small, found that they had unwanted horses. They discovered that only a few types were required. Light horses, general-purpose horses and some of the big types were no longer required, for the reasons I have mentioned. The result is that numbers of these horses are running over the country, eating grass that is needed now for cattle and sheep to produce beef and mutton. Everyone here knows how sorely we need beef and mutton in this country, and indeed how sorely the world at large needs such meat. It is therefore foolish to have horses grazing where you can raise cattle and sheep and produce beef and mutton.
The stockmen were faced with two alternatives. They could hunt down and destroy the horses or make them available either as feed for the fur farmers or as food for human consumption. Let us consider for a moment the first suggestion. If you hunt down and destroy the horses there is an expense involved in the process, while the only return yoii could get would be the hides and bones, and that would not pay. So far as making the horses available to the fur farmers was concerned, there was no possible chance of the fur farms' in this country ever using up the supply. The next thing, therefore, was to find some market for the horses, to sell them to those who would use them as human food. That was done. A survey was made, and hon. members will appreciate that it takes quite a while to do all these things. Even the Department of Agriculture here was called in to assist, and after the survey was made it was found that the Belgians would use horses as food. They are fed on short grass, and there is no better meat if you can make up your mind to eat it. I have not tried it, but * it is used to a large extent.
Here was an opportunity to get rid of the horses, replace them on these ranges by cattle and sheep, and still obtain something in return for the horses. Is that not good business? Is not every private enterprise man here willing to admit that it is only the part of wisdom for men who have produced horses for some time, and gone to the expense involved in their production, to seek to get some return for them? Well, money was required for the necessary processing of the meat. No one man could afford the cost of equipment, processing and so on. No one man could finance the whole undertaking from this country to [Mr. Bentley.1
Belgium. The result was that these people organized a cooperative, and that requires a good deal of work.
These horses were scattered all over western Saskatchewan and a great part of Alberta. The producers had to procure the necessary plant and equipment. The first thing they did was to interview the various horse owners and inquire what they thought of the idea, whether they would like to be members of the cooperative, and then get them to join and to supply capital and ship the horses to the plant. I think hon. members will appreciate how much organizational work would be called for there, the expense involved and the time necessary to make all the preparations. Of course much of the work was not paid for but some had to be paid for. I do not wish to labour the point as regards the work that was done, but my hon. friends who come from Ontario or Quebec can well imagine the amount of travelling that would be necessary in order to interview everyone who might possibly be interested in a similar project in either of those provinces.
They did it. That is the point. They did it and finally they got things going. The plant was set up, and the government of Saskatchewan underwrote the original debt to the extent of $50,000 and gave another guarantee on top of that. The buying commission acting on behalf of the Belgian people made arrangements with the Department of Trade and Commerce and made an advance, but the great bulk of the money was subscribed by the producers in actual cash or in the form of promissory notes. Actual cash, however, was necessary to pay wages and procure machinery. That has been done through the bank, and the amount involved has to be paid back either from earnings of the plant, from the proceeds, or from the pockets of these men.
That has all been taken care of and the plant is still going. Deliveries are being made. The Belgian government takes what it requires as long as the product is packaged as the people there want it. Small cuts are put into cans and sent to UNRRA, and a great deal goes to Poland.
I suggest that it is only just not to tax that cooperative but to treat it as one coming under the provisions set out here, except for the date line to which I have referred. Whenever it suits the purpose of the minister, and he wishes to support an argument he is making, he has recourse to the McDougall report.
I would refer him to page 43 where the following paragraph appears:
It has been pointed out to us on numerous occasions that cooperative associations are difficult to organize-

Income War Tax
I have told you how to organize one.
-and that their rate of mortality is high, especially in their earlier years. They are not in a position to attract capital for investment purposes,-
My investing friends will understand that. -except in small amounts. Moreover, they are apt to find it difficult to finance the employment of the necessary managerial personnel.
That is quite true.
In addition, there is a pronounced tendency to organize cooperatives in times of economic stress. We are, therefore, of the opinion that in the public interest, cooperative associations, upon consent of the minister, should be exempt entirely from income tax during the first few years of their operation.
That is the recommendation by the royal commission, which I think-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: You notice the words there, "upon consent of the minister"?
Exactly, and that is what I am trying to get. I am trying to get the consent of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That implies one of these discretionary powers to which so much exception has been taken, and we have eliminated that.

I would remind the minister that I did not voice those objections. I am trying to "sell" the minister a bill of goods which I think he will like after he gets it, and which the cooperative associations will appreciate.
Let me come back to my illustration. This is what this horse marketing cooperative association does. First, it helps to feed the hungry people overseas. Everyone who gets some of this horse meat would otherwise go hungry. Whether we like it or not, they like it. It removes horses from range and pasture required by sheep and cattle. That is something every man in this country can understand. We require these things because to-day meat is rationed.
The cooperative was financed and equipped in the face of great difficulty. You need only to ask the people who undertook it and they will tell you of the difficulty. It has provided long-term employment for over a hundred additional people in that place. I believe that 125 people are employed there. It is a well-established plant. It is so well laid out that tiny nave a pretty little nurse to take care of cut fingers and so forth.
Oh, oh.

The plant is well equipped. I shall not try to sell the nurse to the minister. The employment provided there is to the advantage not only of the city but of the
country generally. These men are working; they are building houses for themselves. They are taking advantage of all housing plans. A great many of them are returned men because they get a preference, provided that they will take the job and are in physical condition to do the work, which, of course, requires men who are physically fit.
The cooperative stands to make no profit. It hopes only to reimburse to a limited extent owners of surplus horses whose previous reasonable expectation was to get an average price of S50 to $75 per horse, and who realize not more than an average of $25 a horse. I can tell the committee why that is. The horses are brought into the plant by the owners. They are graded according to the kind of flesh that is on them and to the best of the ability of the men who understand how to grade horses. It is not an extensive proposition but they do a pretty good job. For the best horses they can get only two cents a pound, A-reasonably fat horse weighing 1,500 pounds at two cents a pound would bring in $30. Many of them will not bring in that much; the average is around $25. I am being rather generous. From the amount each owner receives is deducted the amount that, he had to subscribe to the capital of the outfit, and it is so much per horse. Then, when the accounts are all made up, each one will be reimbursed according to the number of horses and the pounds of meat he has contributed. It will not be a great deal. I dioubt whether it will average more than four or five dollars per horse, so that in the final analysis it will amount to $30 a horse. Surely no one will say that the men who own these horses are getting too much for the cost of producing the animal before it went to the plant. If we are to tax the outfit and make it much more difficult for them to go on with their work, then all that they have done in the past will be nullified by that three year clause.
When I was speaking on this matter a few days ago the minister said that he did not know much about it. I am going to prove my assertion by making him a little gift of this can of horse meat, just to prove that we have the plant there and are actually operating it. I give it to him with the compliments of the Swift Current horse marketing association. I use it as an illustration, because this is the one of which I know, but there are countless other illustrations all over the country which are in very much the same position. Therefore it should not be too much to expect the government to remove the provision dealing with 1947 and make it the first day of February, 1944, or something along that line
Income War Tax

and thereby remove the fears of these people who have been in this business so long.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: After listening to my hon. friend deal with the problems of the cooperatives, I first want to congratulate the Horse Cooperative Marketing Association Limited of Swift Current for their enterprise and initiative in forming this new association, and I thank my hon. friend for his courtesy in presenting me with his compliments, with this tin of horse meat and gravy.
Are you going to throw a party to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall try it out on my family and see what the result may be. In a more serious vein may I deal with the question which the hon, member has raised as to making this exemption apply to cooperatives which are already in existence. The position is that a somewhat similar concession, if I may call it that, wras given some time ago to the mining industry and is still in existence whereby new mines are exempt from income tax for the first three years after they come into production. At the time that provision was introduced it was urged, as it is urged now, that it should apply pro rata to mines which were already in production; for instance, one started a couple of years before that should get one year more. That was refused because the provision was put into the act as being in the nature of incentive legislation to encourage the opening of new mines. The same principle applies here. It is to encourage the formation of new cooperatives. A similar provision has been inserted which was made applicable to mines whereby new cooperatives would not be subject to income tax for the first three years. It is felt that we should offer the same principle here that we did in the other case. If the cooperative is formed, then the members are already persuaded of the desirability of engaging in that form of enterprise. The capital has been put in, or presumably some of it has been put in, and it is felt that the provision should not be made retroactive but should apply to new cooperatives for the three years after their formation. I may say we gave consideration to ths representations which were made by my hon. friend and also by hon. members on this side of the house that what he is suggesting should be introduced into the law, but it was felt that it could not be done.

If the cooperative is formed it cannot come under this act, because the act is on the books. The minister says that the purpose of this is to encourage new cooperatives, but if a new cooperative is [Mr. B.ntley.J
strangled in six months it is not much encouragement for others to be bom. I think the minister should change that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It will not be strangled as a result of income tax; let me assure my hon. friend of that. It may fail because its customers do not patronize it enough or because it cannot get capital, but no new cooperative will go out of business because of the burden of income tax which is imposed; I can assure my hon. friend of that.

I hope the minister will not take that can of meat and throw it in the garbage pail when he gets home. Last winter, when the university of Saskatchewan held their stock show they did not realize until after the date had been set that they had chosen a meatless day. They usually serve a lunch, and when they were about to decide what they were going to use in the sandwiches they discovered it was a meatless day and they could not have meat sandwiches. Somebody then had a bright idea, which was that horse meat was not included in meatless days or was not considered as meat. The superintendent of the institution sent to Moose Jaw and got a piece of horse meat, and I might say that we all had horse meat sandwiches that day. If we had not known it was horse meat we would not have been any the wiser. The texture is a little coarser than beef and the colour is redder. I am sure that if the minister tries that meat he will enjoy it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am looking forward to it unless my hon. friend wants to take it back.
* Mr. CAMPBELL: No. May we return to the bill? We might be able to change the minister's mind a little further. When the budget was dropped in our laps and the Minister of Finance left for other parts I thought that possibly the acting minister might take a rigid attitude. I thought that, as a result, it would not be possible to have many changes made in these resolutions. I am pleased, however, to see that the minister has not taken that attitude; that he has relaxed to some extent. In a moment I am going to move an amendment which I hope will receive his favourable consideration, but before doing so I want to support the contention of the hon. member for Swift Current that a cooperative should be exempt for three years. The government has accepted that principle, and it was also recommended by the McDougall commission that a cooperative should be exempt for the first three years. You might take a horse meat packing plant, or you might take a cooperative such as we have in a little town close to where I live.

Income War Tax
That cooperative was started last year. Under this section as it stands they are going to be taxed for two years, and we think the government should accept the principle, and support it by legislation, that a cooperative should be exempt from taxation for the first three years. So I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Swift Current, that on page 4 of the bill, paragraph (e), line 12, be amended by striking out the words "after commencement of its business" and in lines 13 and 14 by striking out the words "commencing business on or after the first day of January, nineteen hundred and forty-seven".

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
There is an amendment
already, so that this will have to be a subamendment. I submit, of course, what my hon. friend probably know-s, that this amendment is clearly out of order. If adopted it would diminish the revenue, and as such is an amendment which can be moved only by a member of the government with the approval of His Excellency the Governor General.

May I ask a question
with regard to paragraph (iii), which is now the subject of the amendment to which the minister has already referred. I understand that this will now read "all its members are individuals". Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

Then what will be the position of a cooperative that receives produce for packing, grading and shipping from a farm which is owned by a partnership, a syndicate or even a company? In these packing houses to which I referred when we were discussing the resolutions the produce of quite a number of farms so owned passes through the hands of the cooperatives. Under this wording, does it mean that in future the new cooperative must not accept produce from a firm which is owned by a company?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They could accept the produce of such a firm, of course, but I suppose that would be non-member business, if it were owned by a corporation. I do not know how these things work. I did not know farms were owned by corporations, but perhaps the president might be a member of the cooperative. In any event, for the purposes of this section a corporation cannot be a member of a cooperative if the cooperative is to qualify for this initial three-year tax exemption.

That is where one great difficulty arises in trying to understand these taxation proposals. As far as I know, those twenty or thirty cooperative shipping houses do not have membership. You ship through
them, and in a certain sense a shipper through them is a member of that cooperative outfit. But it does the business of receiving, grading, packing, preparing for shipping and shipping the produce of the orchards and farms all around. The great majority of them are owned by individuals, but certainly there are cases of partnerships. Those are not individuals in the sense of this section.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They would be within the meaning of this section. There is no question about that.
Others are owned by syndicates; I am thinking of one such at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Then all members of the syndicate would be individuals and presumably under those circumstances would be members of the cooperative.

If they shipped their
produce through the cooperative?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right. This would exclude corporations from becoming members of the cooperative for the purpose of this initial three-year exemption. It is not contemplated that this special treatment for cooperative organizations should be extended to organizations which are mere holding companies for other companies, if I may so describe it.

I have waited until the bill got into committee, because quite frankly I could not understand the effect of this proposed legislation when it was in the resolution stage. I should now like to ask the minister some questions in order to try to understand the effect of this legislation. First, I want to .put the case of what I regard as a true cooperative; that is, a producers' cooperative where the business is carried on much as described by the hon. member for Yale. Take the case of a fruit growers' cooperative. They bring their produce to the cooperative. They do not receive an initial payment but merely a credit slip for so many boxes of apples. The cooperative then markets the apples; when it receives payment therefor it makes a distribution of the total proceeds, and each individual receives his proportionate share less his proportionate share of the expenses. What I do not understand is how that cooperative can be liable to pay any income tax at all, because I do not see that it has any income. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend; I do not think it has any taxable income at all under the conditions he has outlined. In substance, it is simply accepting the produce
Income War Tax

on consignment, marketing it, deducting the expenses and remitting the balance to its members. I quite agree with my hon. friend that under those circumstances there would be no taxable income whatever.
I do not want to appear to be guilty of trying to catch the minister, because this is important, I think, when we come to the three per cent provision a little later on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If you want to cover that now, there would be no three per cent payment either, because there would be no taxable income out of which to make it.

That is what I want to understand. This cooperative may have $40,000 or $50,000 worth of plant, to which the members have subscribed initially. In the case I am thinking of, the cooperative has its packing plant and a box factory as well, so I should like to have that clear. If it carries on its business in that way there is no taxable income in the hands of the cooperative; the income is not taxable until it has reached the hands of the individual members?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is quite correct. On the hypothetical case my hon. friend has put forward the cooperative would have no taxable income and, therefore, there would be no tax. In the same way the three per cent rule could not apply because there would be no income out of which three per cent could be attributed as a return on capital.
But there is capital.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I made that point clear in connection with the resolutions, that a cooperative may have employed capital; but its way of doing business may be such, the contracts it makes with its customers may be such that it ends the year without any taxable income, and if it has no taxable income, then it pays no income tax. There are plenty of other organizations which may have employed capital of $100,000 or S200.000 or $500,000 which pay no tax unless they earn taxable income.
That is what I thought, and I am glad to have the minister confirm it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I want to make that perfectly. clear. Mind you, it is only in a case such as my hon. friend suggests, where business is done in that way, that this result would follow; but in the case he has cited there would be no taxable income and the section would not apply.

May I remind the minister of the illustration I gave when this matter was before the committee in the resolution stage? Such a cooperative, for the benefit 
of its members, sets up a store in which it sells a great variety of things. At the end of the year the members of that cooperative receive a rebate on the amount of their purchases. That may be a first cousin to the patronage dividend which is used here.
But the public also shops at the store, and the amount of rebate paid back to the customers who are not shippers through the cooperative is a form of profit. That being the case,- and this concern earning a profit on a fraction of its main business, does it get caught under this three per cent provision? It is an organization which, on a small portion of its business, has made a profit. Surely it cannot be mulcted to the extent of three per cent on its capital.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The case which my hon. friend has set out is that of a consumer cooperative. It is a cooperative which provides its members with groceries.
It is a small subsidiary of a large producer cooperative.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes. On that business which it does, if it returns to its customers a portion of its profits-and for want of a better term I shall call them profits-that is in effect a patronage dividend, and it is deductible from gross income under the bill now before the committee. If the same payment is made to non-members, that is deductible, too. Whatever payment is made to non-members is deductible.
But if I understood correctly the facts as my hon. friend recited them, the three per cent rule would apply there to the extent that the cooperative had employed capital. If the small cooperative which my hon. friend mentions had employed capital of $10,000, within the definition, three per cent on $10,000 would be $300, and it might be taxed $90. That is the extent of the tax, before it could distribute patronage dividends.
Would they be allowed to keep those two businesses separate for taxation purposes-their producer cooperative and packing-plant business on the one hand, and the little store on the other?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is somewhat difficult to answer that offhand. I should think they would not have any income in the one case, and in the other case they would have comparatively small income, which would be subject to tax.

If I followed the minister correctly, I understood him to say that the three per cent would apply only to that portion of the cooperative which is used for that small subsidiary business.

Income Tl'ar Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, I do not think so. I think you would have to look at the cooperative as a whole. If it could so arrange its business that it had no income with respect to its producer operations, but could not so arrange it that it had no income with respect to its consumer operations, it might have to pay a small tax under the three per cent rule. But it is most difficult to give a definite answer on a hypothetical case without having all the circumstances before me.

But does the minister not see in my illustration that the only profit is made on a part of the business of the subsidiary, and the subsidiary itself is but a small part of the far larger cooperative organization. There may be half a million dollars in the cooperative organization-the packing house, cold storage plant and that sort of thing. But perhaps there is only about $10,000 of its capital used in this subsidiary that is selling groceries. Only a fraction of that can be called profit on the produce which is sold to non-shippers.
Have I not made plain to the minister that it is contrary to common sense that this organization of half a million dollars should be mulcted of three per cent of that capital because it has made profits on a small part of the business of its subsidiary.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is mulcted of three per cent of that capital. Three per cent of that capital is considered as taxable income. The whole three per cent is not taken. Three per cent is considered as taxable income, and a tax may be exigible. If the income is not there, there is no tax possible.
We say that three per cent of half a million dollars is $15,000. Let us suppose, on balance, that the little consumer ends up with a net income of $2,000. You could not tax on the

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee on bill No. 368, to amend the Income War Tax Act-Mr. Abbott-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 4, subsection 1-Depletion.

The question I have to ask the minister at this stage is based on the last three lines of this section, and that is the power given to the officials of the department. The language is quite specific: "The minister shall have full power to apportion the deduction between them and his determination shall be conclusive." With regard to the exhaustion or depletion of a mine or timber limit, we are by this clause giving, if I may say so, extreme powers to the department, and I suggest to the minister that the appointment of a referee on the question of depletion might be advantageous. I realize, of course, that this is a technical matter, but since, under the wording of the present section, the supreme and absolute verdict is with the minister and his department-	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is only as to apportionment.

Yes, only as to apportionment.

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He acts as a referee if they cannot agree among themselves. Where the lessor and lessee disagree the minister comes in. Somebody has to act as referee.
I suggest that a referee be appointed where they cannot agree. I realize that this is not a question of the minister disagreeing in a case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This has been in the act for a great many years and there has never been any difficulty. The lessor and lessee, in case of disagreement, have apparently always been willing to accept the minister and so describe him. Somebody gets the full depletion allowance and, where there is a case of lessor and lessee, normally the lessor would get it. But it might, be appropriate that it should be divided between the lessor and the lessee. If they can agree as to how the full depletion allowance is to be apportioned, well and good; that disposes of the matter. If they cannot agree the minister is in effect appointed sole arbitrator. That is the effect of this particular section. That is all it is.
What machinery does the minister use? I can understand that the minister cannot himself sit on these questions. What in effect happens when there is disagreement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: When there is a dispute the deputy minister or an official designated by him hears both parties, as any other arbitrator would do, and then makes a finding. In effect, he is acting as arbitrator. If the parties can agree among themselves there is nothing to do; their agreement makes the law, as it were. But if they cannot agree, then the minister is appointed arbitrator, and in normal circumstances he would act through his deputy minister or some appropriate official. I am advised that it has worked very well on that phase for a great many years. [DOT] It has been in the law for a good many years, and it is safe to say it is pretty generally accepted by those affected as a reasonable provision.
I realize it has worked, I will not say with entire satisfaction. But it has been an old clause in the act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend will no doubt have noticed that in this section we are taking out the provision which gave the minister discretion to determine the amount which may be fixed as depletion and providing that it shall be determined by the governor in council, that is, by order in council. Of course that will be made public to all concerned.
That means the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It means the cabinet. It means that the governor in council will establish rates of depletion, and we believe that is better than leaving it to a single minister. On reflection, I believe my hon. friend will agree that that is desirable. Someone has to fix the rates. It is not desirable to fix them in the statute, because it might be well to vary them from time to time. They will be fixed in future by order in council, and that will be made available to all interested. It will be public property.
But the order in council, once passed, is a final act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It could be varied a month later if that were desirable.
But my suggestion is that if the order in council is passed the contestants or disputants have no chance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That just fixes the rate of depletion. Previously the minister fixed the rate. One man fixed the rate, and it has always been urged that it was not fixed by the minister but by the officials. I do not agree with that, but that has been the contention. Under the new procedure the rate will be fixed by the governor in council; then under the discretion clause at the end, if it is a case of lessor and lessee of these mining, oil or timber limits, if the lessor and the lessee cannot agree as to how the twenty or thirty per cent is to be divided, the minister acts as sole arbitrator. That is the effect of the section.

In fact what it really boils down to is that the treasury board decides.

nothing to do with the matter.

Mr.	ABBOTT:	It is	a cabinet	decision
instead of a departmental decision.

Could you fix a different amount for different mines? Do they vary in each individual case, or is there a general rule?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A general rule is laid down; but if, for instance in the case of a coal mine, they could show that there is a definite coal deposit for which they paid a definite price, then that could be dealt with as a special case. That is one of the reasons; the other is for the owner to get as much as he can in depreciation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a business argument.

This section has to do with base metal mines, and inasmuch as the general reasoning behind the price of gold was made a subject matter in this debate I wonder whether the minister could enlighten the committee-because I am sure as many members are in the dark as I am- as to just why the government does not allow producers of base metals, such as copper, lead and zinc to obtain the world price for these commodities and in that wray help not only the old mines but also the new ones.

We can understand that, because wTe are endeavouring to maintain a domestic price ceiling, but so far as the export of these commodities is concerned-and we are substantial exporters of copper, lead and zinc-it seems strange to the uninformed at least that the price which our producers get should be so much below the world prices.

On section 4, subsection 2-Exemptions and deductions.

Though I had not intended to take part in the debate on the bill now before the committee, I wish, however, 
to make a few remarks on this subsection to-night. Like the great majority of taxpayers of this country, I should have liked to see in the bill greater exemptions to taxpayers in the lower income tax bracket. I, on the other hand, fully understand and realize the need for this government to raise the necessary funds for the administration of the country during these years immediately following a long and arduous war period with still heavy commitments resulting therefrom. I most heartily welcome the substantial reductions made in this bill, and I most particularly appreciate the fact that these reductions are inversely proportionate to the scale of the various incomes affected.
We are told that the total loss of revenue to the treasury can be safely estimated at an annual amount of approximately $150 million. I take pleasure in thanking the government for having been able to realize this substantial reduction in taxation, and I hope that succeeding budgets will1 gradually increase the rate of this relaxation in the taxation policy of this government. Like other hon. members, I, during the past two months, have received numerous representations asking that all personal income below $3,000' be exempt from taxation. Most of these representations were formulated on the hundreds of post cards of the type which I now hold in my hand, and which every member of the committee easily recognizes. In connection with these postcards, I received last week a letter, the contents of which I consider it my duty to make public at this stage of the discussion. The letter I wush to refer to enclosed one of these cards, and, since the letter was originally written in French, I am giving the committee as close a translation as possible. The letter reads as follows:
Cortereal, July 24, 1946. Mr. L. Langlois, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Last Sunday two men came to our church meeting with these post cards which they were selling five cents apiece .urging us to send these cards to our member of parliament in order to help him obtain the abolition of income tax. They call this organization "L'Union des Eleeteurs" (Union of Electors). It is supposed to help you to obtain from the government what your electors demand. Is this good or not? Would you be kind enough to let me know as soon as possible, please, as these gentlemen will again be here during the month of August and if it is good I would like to work with them. Hoping to receive your reply at your earliest convenience, I thank you and remain,
Yours very truly,
Armand Lacombe,
St. Majorique, Cortereal, County of Gaspe.
The contents of this letter are confirmed in the number of June 1, 1946, of the paper

Income War Tax
Vers Demain, published at Beauceville-Est, Quebec, by "L'Unioa Creditiste des Electeurs de la province de Quebec."
In this number of June 1 of the said paper, I read on page 2 the following advertisement. Pressure Cards.
Your federal member was in receipt of $4,000 a year of which $1,200 was exempt from income tax. He found himself badly paid. In the space of. a few minutes he and his colleagues of Ottawa voted a bill to give themselves an increase of $2,000 entirely exempted from income tax. Your federal member, therefore, now receives $6,000 a year, of which $3,200 is free from income tax. Good for him but he should think of his electors. The electors are as much entitled as the member to live. Your member is selfish and has no heart if he does not claim with all the power and strength he possesses the exemption of income tax for every person whose revenue does not exceed $3,000. This is what you must tell him again and again.
Write now to your member to get your small income free from income tax. The office of Vers Demain has postal cards printed to express this demand. The only thing you have to do is to write the name of ycriir member on one side and sign your name on the other. No postage stamp is required. Order these cards in great number and sell them ai'ound in your neighbourhood. Urge and have others urge your members with these claims for his electors.
Pressure cards, each	$0 05
25 cards for	1 00
Address your order to Union des Electeurs,
C.P. 71 Station Delorimier,
Montreal, P.Q.
This is as nearly as possible a translation of the advertisement published in the said paper, which is the official paper of L'Union des Electeurs. From the letter I read a few moments ago it will be seen that this organization has now placed commercial salesmen on the road to promote the sale of these post cards. In case some hon. members do not know the organization calling itself L'Union des Electeurs, I add that this organization is a cover name for the Social Credit party in the province of Quebec, the head of which is none other than the national vice-president of the Social Credit party, Mr. J. Ernest Gregoire, former mayor of Quebec city. I am informed that the cost of these cards can safely be estimated, if printed in great quantities, at approximately one cent each, including the material. Therefore, if one makes the subtraction from the price at which these cards were sold, one can realize that the net profit made on each card by this organization which is selling them in the province of Quebec to-day, is four cents. I feel it my duty to denounce this scandalous exploitation of the public, and I ask the Minister of National Revenue to tell this committee whether or not the Social Credit party, or L'Union des Electeurs of the province of 63260-299J
Quebec, are making income tax returns, since it would appear that this party is running a profit-making enterprise in that province.
Where do you get your slush funds?

I know that my statement hurts my hon. friend, but he is not through with it yet. Every member of this house can easily see, by the number of cards he has received, how much this party has made by selling these cards to his electors, who in turn address them to him. I must also add that this house and the public in general expect from the leader of the Social Credit party some explanation of such conduct on the part of his followers in Quebec, and, most of all, his national vice-president, Mr. Gregoire. We also expect him to tell this committee whether or not he approves such conduct. As hon. members no doubt have noticed, the last paragraph on the post card to my mind contains a threat to elected members of this house. The paragraph in question reads as follows, and I shall translate. This is addressed to the members of this house:
And please take notice that if you do not proceed with rapidity and tenacity I shall be obliged to refuse to vote for you at the next election.
I beg to refer the committee to paragraph 201, Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, 3rd edition, on page 85, which reads:
In the Commons, on the 12th April, 1733, and. on the 1st June, 1780, it was resolved that it was a high infringement of the privilege of the house, a crime and misdemeanour, to assault,, insult or menace any member of the house, ini his coming or going from the house, or upon the account of his behaviour in parliament; or to endeavour-
I underline this.
-to compel members of declare themselves in favour of or against any proposition then depending, or expected to be brought before the house.
I might add that the electoral instructions also contain a similar disposition. I submit that L'Union des Electeurs, or the Quebec Social Credit party, are guilty of this infringement on the privileges of members of this house. The leader of the Social Credit party cannot pretend that this was done by members of his party who are not in authority, because it was done by the head of L'Union des Electeurs, who now acts as his righthand man, being vice-president of his party for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I commented on this at some length a year ago when the provision was first inserted. The hon. member will notice that the wording in the statute is "unusual medical expenses". It was never considered appropriate that a man should deduct from his income the amount of his ordinary medical expenses; that is part of the expense of living. But is was felt that in cases where an individual was put to expenditure entirely beyond the ordinary amount of medical expenses, some relief should be given by permitting that excess to be deducted from income; and it was thought that, broadly speaking, four per cent of a man's income was a not unreasonable amount to treat as normal medical and dental expenses to which one would be put. Of course no act is perfect. I do not know that my formula would improve the situation, but I am sure the minister will 
agree that the present act lends itself to considerable fraud. I am speaking from some knowledge when I say that certain fees are settled for certain amounts if no receipt is given. With this method, as the average person does not expect to reach the allowable amount, he does not get receipts; maybe he should. I am speaking of a means which I think might be employed to the advantage of all and would still result in the same amount of revenue for the government.

There are two matters to which I should like to draw the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance. I was bold enough to put them before the Minister ol Finance last fall; I hope the acting ministei will be a little more receptive than the ministei was then. I contend that is an anomaly which ought to be corrected. I cannot see any justification for it in principle. As I understand it, the reason given by the department hitherto is that it is difficult to administer, that you might have frauds perpetrated by taxpayers acting in concert with druggists. Surely the danger is no greater than that of taxpayers working in combination with physicians, for that matter.

But if the wife earned $1 more, namely $750, then the husband will lose the benefit of the full $750 deduction. Surely there is an anomaly there. If you are going to make a difference of $251 in the result as respects deductions from the husband's income when the wife earns that $1 more, being the difference between $749 and $750, it does not seem right.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think the correct interpretation is that the extent to which the wife's income runs over $250 is deducted from the husband's exemption, and that continues to the point where the husband and the wife each, have an exemption of $750, or are treated as single persons for income tax purposes.

I wish to speak briefly on this item, since I feel that it will adversely affect practically every industry in the county I represent. In the canning industry a great portion of the work has always been done by women, to the extent that one-half of the people employed in the canneries to-day are women, and quite a large proportion are married women. This work cannot be done by men. To-day the production of food is one of the major problems confronting the world, and I believe that this regulation will have a tendency to curtail production at a time when every effort should be made to increase it, particularly canned goods, since they can be shipped to any part of the world where people might be faced with starvation or famine.
If this change would result in taking married women out of jobs that could be filled by war veterans and married men seeking employment I would support it 100 per cent, but that is not the case in the three large industries in the county of Charlotte, all of which will be affected by this measure. I speak particularly of the canning industry, which, as I said before, employes hundreds of married women. I would refer also to Canada Cottons at Milltown, Charlotte county, and Ganong Brothers; and there are many smaller industries engaged in the smoking, skinning and so on of herring, particularly on Grand Manan island, where a great many of the girls and women employed are married.
My argument is that from the point of view of revenue I feel confident this regulation will be responsible for a loss rather than any gain to the government. Take, for example, a married woman employed in the canning industry in which, as I have already said, much of the work can be done only by women. Let us say she is able to make $5 a day,

Income War Tax
which many of these women are earning in the canneries at the present time. I am sure the proposed tax would not be more than S2. Under ordinary conditions this same woman can pack twenty-five cases of sardines a day. The wholesale value of twenty-five cases of Sardines would be not less than $150, on which the sales tax would be $12. Suppose this woman refuses to work owing to the increased taxes. This government, by insisting on the collection of $2 in income tax, will lose the $12 in sales tax. I can assure the minister that this condition will exist in Charlotte county when this regulation goes into force, and it would appear to me to be exactly the same circumstances in which the dog found himself when he reached for the shadow and, in doing so, lost the bone.
Since I do not believe in criticizing without suggesting some solution, and while this is perhaps an unusual case, I would suggest that married women engaged in seasonal work or on piecework be exempt from this regulation. My reason for suggesting this exemption is that married women doing this type of work are in a position to regulate their earnings to coincide with the exemptions set out in the regulations, and without doubt it will be responsible for a great reduction in the production of necessary food and other commodities much needed at the present time.
Another matter was brought to my attention only this evening by a gentleman from my own county whose wife is a schoolteacher. She had agreed with the school board in the town of St. Stephen to teach during the coming term, owing to the scarcity of teachers all over that province. .When thiis regulation was announced in the press she went back to the school board and told them she would not teach. I am told that at the present time they are looking everywhere for schoolteachers. I know the same condition existed in New Brunswick during the war, when we had perforce to get married women to go back into the schools, and I feel that this regulation will have an adverse effect in that direction also, for I am sure that many schoolteachers who are also married women will refuse to work under these conditions.

I would suggest to the minister, as I intended to do on the resolution but did not, that the exempted $250 be applied only to investment income, and that the exempted income from earnings be increased to $500. I believe that would overcome the abjections raised by the last speaker and would overcome the abjection in the cities where women go out for cleaning and other work which takes only part of their time but which

is absolutely essential. I believe there should be a difference in the treatment given investment income and that given income earned by hard work, and I think if the minister would accept this amendment it would overcame many of the objections to this regulation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The $250 is to cover any kind of income, whether investment or earned, but over that figure the exemption of the husband is reduced proportionately. I do not believe we would be justified in making a distinction over $250 between an earned income and investment income.
There is a great deal of distinction in actual life between the person who gets three per cent on $8,000 and the woman who goes out and slaves at cleaning and other manual work.
Previously the minister said this exemption was introduced during the war in order to encourage women to work. Is the present regulation being put in now to discourage them from working?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. It was an exceptional provision,- one which would not normally be part of an income tax structure and one which really cannot be justified on the ground of fairness as between different taxpayers. It was put in as a bit of bait, if I may use a somewhat vulgar phrase, but it is not a fair provision as between all taxpayers in this country, and should not be .part of a permanent income tax structure. That is the point I am making.

Under the set-up in 1947 there will be a difference of only $180; that is how much better off they would be if they were each earning incomes of $750, or $660 as it is at the present time. They would gain $180; but when you apply this $250 clause and the married woman earns just $750, in 1947 she will be away in the hole in comparison with her position at the present time. It makes a big difference. There is a difference of $410 between the $250 and the $660.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is true there will not be the same tax incentive; there will be more taxes to pay, but the joint exemption under the act in certain cases could go up almost to $2,500.
How do you get that between the two of them, when the exemption is only $660 each?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Well, I am sorry; it is $1,860.

Then my small town friends across the way are talking for political purposes only.

When the resolutions were before the house I told the minister that I objected to this three per cent clause. I still feel the same way about it. I pleaded with the minister to make some concessions in the matter, but evidently I have not a pleading way, because he never listened. I want the minister to know that I do object to that, because you are driving the cooperatives to be a profit-making class, which they are not in. I have said that before, and I know that no one will want me to repeat my arguments, but I have a couple of matters which I want to straighten out. Take a cooperative whose employed capital amounted to $100,000; they would pay three per cent on that, or $3,000; w'ould they be taxed thirty per cent on that $3,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Only if they had $3,000 of taxable income. They could have $100,000 of employed capital, but if their affairs were so arranged or the cooperative operated in such a way that they did not have taxable income-

Well, I wish the minister would let me finish, because I am at a disadvantage; when you get a dirt farmer up against a lawyer you pretty well knock him off his thinking. In that instance we will assume that the cooperative had $10,000 of savings, and we divided $8,000 to the members in patronage dividends and had $2,000 left; would that cooperative pay three p'er cent on the $2,000, or would they pay three per cent on $3,000?

speechtext: If the $10,000 which my hon. friend mentioned were taxable income within the meaning of the act they would pay on $3,000. They could distribute $7,000 as patronage dividends and deduct that in full, but they would be obliged to pay the tax on $3,000 before distributing the balance as patronage dividends.
I said $8,000 and $2,000 left.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They could have distributed the extra $1,000, but they would be liable to pay tax on it.
Take the next year, with this same turnover of business. We distribute $6,000 in patronage dividends and we have $4,000 left. Will we pay three per cent on $4,000 or on the $3,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: You will pay tax on $4,000 because that would not have been allocated but would have been held in reserve I suppose. The permissible distribution and the deduction which would be allowed on the figures the hon. gentleman has given would be $7,000 distributed as patronage dividends tax free and the $3,000 would be subject to tax.
That means that if the cooperative made no savings at all, if it suffered a loss, it would still have to pay 3 per cent on its working capital?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. If it suffers a loss there is no tax on the capital employed. That is the point I made this afternoon in answer to the hon. member for Yale. There is no tax on income if there is no income. That is the test. If a cooperative is earning no income at all or suffers a loss, or if it so arranges its affairs that there is no taxable income, the three per cent does not apply, and that will be the case I am certain with a good many cooperatives.

I still think it is not right. I have been a cooperator all my life. As I said here, I was born in a cooperative home, and I cannot for the life of me see why you drive the cooperatives into the profit-making class where we never had any right to belong.

Is this three per cent a baby of the Department of Finance, or is it an illegitimate child sponsored by the Department of Finance and1 fathered by Winnipeg and Toronto organizations? In my opinion this has been brought about by pressure from outside from organizations opposed to the wheat pool and cooperative organizations. If the minister and his colleagues will read the newspapers they will find that there is at present in the prairie provinces at least action being prepared that should make the members here sit up and take notice. I have frequently expressed my opposition to this move. I do not think it is in the interest of the country. As I have pointed out time and again, the farmers have been robbed quite enough by the prices they have been forced to take for their produce, without this robbery or confiscation being extended still farther. I want to make it quite clear that I am definitely opposed to this three per cent tax.

I should like to ask the minister a question. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I used to charge a lot of money for giving advice, but I doubt if there is any way of doing that if it waited until the end1 of the year. speechtext:
I want to ask another question. Let us assume that there are two cooperative organizations the same in every respect save in the way in which they distribute their earnings or savings or profits, or whatever you choose to call them. One of them says:	"We propose to distribute all

In the case of the other cooperative, its interest would be paid to the members. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My question is a perfectly fair one-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not suggesting it is not.

But the minister said part of it is not taxable if you pay it all out in patronage dividends. You have to keep enough to pay-

A great many do have capital in the form of dividenthpaying shares or in the form of interest-bearing securities of one sort or another.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I did not get up to argue this point but only to get a straight answer to a straightforward question. Is a cooperative which pays out all its earnings or savings or profits in the form of patronage dividends taxable or not?

speechtext: The law as proposed here is that- a cooperative cannot pay out all its earnings in patronage dividends if it has employed capital.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then here is another cooperative, constructed in the same way, 'but they say, "We will pay our members three per cent interest and, if there is any more to pay out, we will pay that out in patronage dividends". Will that cooperative pay you taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They will not pay us taxes, but they have less to pay in patronage dividends.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You say that in the one case they pay taxes and in the other they do not pay taxes. Ordinarily the purpose of a taxing law is to raise revenue, but what is this government doing? It is bringing in a policy which may not raise revenue at all, because it says to the cooperatives, "If you continue to pay out your earnings as patronage dividends you will be taxed", but it says also, "If you pay it out as interest you will not be taxed". What is the government doing? It is accomplishing nothing but this, the driving of people from cooperative methods into something else. It is obviously not a taxation law at all.

I am glad the leader of the opposition spoke as he did, because I believe he bears out what we have been trying to say in this corner of the house, and that is that the proposed object of the bill seems to be to drive the cooperative movement into the category of profit-making enterprise. I believe this is the pivot of the whole bill, this three per cent argument, and that is why I propose to say something on it.
In the first place, I was interested in listening to-day, on another item, to what the minister said, that we cannot make a distinction between income that is earned and income that is derived from investment. I thought that sounded a little strange coming from a good Liberal, so I sent for Adam Smith's "Wealth of Nations," published in 1776, upon which I understand much of Liberalism is based, because I have always understood, as anyone who studies any economics at all understands, that there is a difference between income earned and income derived from investment. If we refer to Adam Smith's book we shall find a statement which goes back a long way and shows how far Liberalism has strayed from the actual theory on which it is supposed to rest, I quote the following from page 35:
Labour, alone, therefore, never varying in its own value, is alone the ultimate and real standard by which the value of all commodities can at all times and places be estimated and compared. It is their real price; money is their nominal price only.
That means that there is only one source of wealth, namely labour. In other words, there is only one source of income in the long run, and that is income which is earned. Income from investment is only secondary and incidental income which is derived from somebody else's labour. That is a fundamental principle that good Liberals should be willing to accept. I am surprised that the acting minister does not accept it, because even one of our good friends of the Progressive Conservative party to-night accepted that theory, when the hon. member for High Park suggested that income derived from work should be treated differently from income derived from investment. I congratulate him on his socialist outlook, and I congratulate also the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, for he, too, is coming our way.
