What I wish to refer to particularly is this. The whole three per cent question is based upon capital employed. I have tried on several occasions to find out how we can arrive at what is meant by capital employed and I have not been successful. At the top of page 16 of the bill hon. members will find "capital employed in the business" defined in paragraph (b) as follows:
"capital employed in the business" shall be computed in accordance with the first schedule to the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940.
If we turn to the first schedule of the Excess Profits Tax Act of 1940 and examine it we shall find that there are four categories of capital employed in the business under this definition: (a) cost of assets, and it states what that means; (b) accounts receivable less reserve for bad debts; (c) value of assets acquired otherwise than by purchase; and (d) amount of money and bank deposits. To the last one I should like to direct the attention of the committee-the amount of money or bank deposits actually used by the taxpayer in the business.
It is well known that in most cases cooperatives do not begin with large capital investment. They try to carry on business with as little capital as possible. It could then be construed, if anyone wished to do so, that every dollar which comes across the counter, in the case of a consumer's cooperative, and which is used to carry on business, to buy goods from the wholesale cooperative, or from any wholesale, is capital employed in accordance with paragraph (d) of this definition. If that were the ease then the amount of capital employed in the business would be a much greater sum than is generally accepted or expected. I hope the minister will clear that up for us.
A great deal has been said' to find out why the government are so adamant in regard to maintaining this three per cent position. They have been willing to withdraw from some of the ground that they have taken before and to acquiesce in some of the amendments presented. The key to the whole thing is to be found in the remarks of the Minister of Finance when he made his budget speech on June 27 of this year and when he said, as reptorted at page 2921 of Hansard:
The principle underlying this rule is that amounts set aside out of taxable income to be distributed in proportion to patronage by a cooperative or company which does not pay at least three per cent on the capital employed in its business contain earnings which arise from the employment of captal and ought not to escape tax entirely.
That brings me back to what I started with, namely, that the government have now come 
to the position where they are going to make the cooperatives say, or are putting the cooperatives in the position where they will have to admit, that money earns money, something which the cooperatives repudiated from the time they were first organized.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not necessarily that money earns money.
That is practically what the minister said. He said that this money has come out of the employment of capital and ought not to escape, tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It may be elevators or it may be warehouses.

Yes, but that is not the way it has been explained to us in the discussion. What- it means is that the cooperative associations which believe in service at cost are to be forced into the position of having to admit that money is the governing factor in these societies. They will have to admit that money makes money, something incidentally which Adam Smith repudiated in 1776 when he pointed out that money does not earn money; that the only source of wealth is labour applied to natural resources. In this day and age we find that the government which only about a year ago blazoned forth in large letters that they were going to bring in a new social order in Canada, have now repudiated the very basis of their own Liberalism and are not bringing in a new social order. They are going back

I do not know whether they are going backward or forward; they do not know either; they are going somewhere, but far from the basis of Liberalism.
I condemn this with the strongest words at my disposal, because I believe that everything that has been said here points to the fact that there were outside influences at work. The Acting Minister of Finance says there were no influences from outside sources.
I have to take his word for it; but I happen to know something about the campaign which has been carried on by the income tax payers' association. I know' that the basic thing which they want to accomplish is not the collection of a few piffling dollars for the public treasury, to use the words of the Minister of Veterans Affairs-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In what respect is the government going back?

What they wanted to accomplish was to force the cooperative associations of Canada into the position where they would have to acquiesce in this legislation and agree to or admit or accept the principle that money makes money, something which the cooperatives have been trying to

Income War Tax
get away from all these years. The government are going to destroy the very basis upon which cooperation is based.

I should like to say a word on this section. I appreciate that hon. members would like to see this section carried after just one side of the question has been presented.	_
With respect to the government driving the cooperatives into a profit-making organization, may I say that my interpretation is quite different. If anything, the government is leaning backward to assist the cooperatives by allowing them to enjoy exemption from income tax on their profits for the first three years to establish themselves in business. If there is no profit to be made and if the cooperatives are against the principle of using money to make money there is no need for them to show a profit. If they do not show a profit they will have no income tax to pay. That is as concise a statement of the picture as I can present it. It is purely a matter of principle. If the cooperatives and those who are interested in cooperative business say they do not want to make a profit, and if they do not take a profit they do not have to pay tax.
In regard to the question of capital employed, why should they not pay interest on capital employed? May I correct my hon. friend who referred to assets such as merchandise, bills receivable and cash on hand. No doubt he had reference to loans. That is all capital employed. That is the basis of the term "surplus" or "capital employed" as it applies to income tax. That is the recognized base on which you make up your tax returns and also your balance sheet, which you must present if you are borrowing money from a bank, as many of us have to do. The bank asks for your balance sheet. It looks over your assets and liabilities, and the difference between one and the other gives the surplus or capital employed.
The private enterpriser-and I am one of them-is obliged to pay either directly or indirectly on the amount of capital invested in his business from the day he goes into business. What happens to the cooperatives? There are allowed three years' exemption and do not have to face the same situation as the private enterpriser. Therefore I say it is a distinct advantage which the government is offering to the cooperative as against private enterprise.
My hon. friend also referred to the fact that you may consider capital employed in connection with every dollar which goes over the counter. Again I say he shows his lack of
experience. One is a direct exchange, money, the medium of exchange for commodities or goods sold by the merchant whether he is a free enterpriser or a cooperative. That is not capital employed; it is just an exchange medium for the goods. One person is on one side of the counter and the other stands behind the counter. The one behind the counter passes out his goods and the other passes over his money or the medium of exchange, which goes on to the manufacturer. It is not capital employed. My first explanation is the real capital employed, which the cooperative enjoys, while the free enterpriser must pay on the day he goes into business.
I just wished to make these few observations to show that there is a definite difference of opinion in regard to this matter and it is not all one-sided. As a supporter of the government, if I had any criticism to offer, I would say that the government in its offer is leaning too far backwards to satisfy the cooperatives owing to the pressure that has been put on in parliament. It is true that the income tax payers' association have sent out a lot of propaganda, but I do not think the average person took very much stock of it. He did not take any more stock of it than the average person took of the barrage which was put across by the cooperatives. Therefore the benefit derived by either the tax payers' association or those supporting free enterprise or the cooperatives can be discounted. I repeat that the government has gone far in trying to meet the wishes of the cooperatives and has given them an actual handicap with which the free enterpriser has to contend.

I should like to reply to one statement made by the hon. gentleman which I do not think is quite correct. He referred to a barrage by the cooperative associations. In all fairness, I think he should admit that the cooperative associations of this country did not do any lobbying or put any pressure on the members of this house at all-
Oh, oh.
Before you begin to laugh-
It was not necessary in your case, perhaps.

They did not do so until they found it necessary to defend themselves from those who were attacking the very basis of their existence. Then naturally they had to dispel the propaganda being put out against them. Before I sit down, I want to reiterate that I am not criticizing the government for
Income War Tax

not having leaned far enough backward. The way they lean I am afraid that some time they will go back so far they will end with a catastrophe.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No danger.

I am not trying to win any more concessions from the government in connection with this bill. I think we have reached a deadlock and there is no use talking about the matter much longer. But I am making a wholesale condemnation of the motives behind the bill itself. For the benefit of the senior hon. member for Halifax, who seems to be trying to persuade me that there is such a 'thing as earnings on capital, I want to say I repudiate that idea. I go back to Adam Smith again, at page 66. Listen to his words:
In that original state of things, which precedes both the appropriation of land and the accumulation of stock, the whole produce of labour belongs to the labourer. He has neither landlord nor master to share with him.
That ought to be something for the hon. member to think over. If we were to go back to the original basis of things-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is that you are reading from?

The "Wealth of Nations", by Adam Smith; not Adam, but Adam Smith. One of the reasons I enjoy listening to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario is that he often makes the statement that we should go back to fundamentals, back to the practical things of life. Certainly here is one place where we should go back to the fundamentals; that is, that the wealth produced by labour belongs to labour in the first place. The only way private enterprise or capitalism or whatever you want to call it could make any claim at all was because they had got themselves into the position where they expect to profit from the labour of others. To-day they are trying to deny to the people who produce the wealth the privilege of retaining that wealth. They say no; three per cent of it must be paid out as earnings on capital, which is a myth and which has no basis in any economics. It is a myth created by capitalism in order to make people feel that money creates wealth, and I repudiate that argument.

I should like to follow up the question asked by the leader of the opposition, who brought out in a different way some of the things we have been trying to point out. In the first place, I agree that this is bad law. If I correctly understood the replies of the minister to the leader of the opposition, he told the hon. gentleman that if one coopera-

five over here pays all its money in patronage dividends, then the last four lines of this subsection would apply. They must first be taxable on three per cent of the capital employed; but if the other cooperative over there were to pay out the money by way of interest, they would not be taxable. That was the answer, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not all out in the way of interest.
That is the way I understood the reply to the question.	-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend had better finish what he has to say, and then I shall have my say.

I shall give an example, taking two cooperatives and bringing them down to plain figures. Each has an employed capital of $1,000. At the end of the j^ear each finds that it has earned three per cent, which means that each has earned $30. The first one says, "We will pay it out in patronage dividends on the basis of the business done with the cooperative during the year." The second one says, "We will pay it out on the basis of three per cent of the capital employed." The first one is not taxable. The second one must first declare three per cent of its employed capital before it can pay out any money. Consequently it cannot pay out anything until it has paid three per cent of that $30.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No. In the case of dividends there is no difference between the two companies. They are treated in exactly the same way. A great many cooperatives do have capital in the form of shares, on which they pay dividends, and some have capital in the form of borrowed money on which they pay interest. The leader of the opposition quite properly and perhaps shrewdly took the case of a cooperative which has interest-bearing indebtedness on which it pays interest, and he compared that with the case of a cooperative which had no capital in the form of shares or interest-bearing indebtedness. The hon. gentleman said that in the one case, the case of the company which had part of its capital or all of it in the form of interest-bearing indebtedness, it can deduct that interest from its gross earnings and pay out the balance in patronage dividends, and it will not pay any corporation income tax. The other cooperative, on the other hand, which earns exactly the same amount and which has employed capital of the same amount-the hon. gentleman used the figure of $100,000-but whose employed capital is in the form of neither shares nor borrowed capital, cannot pay out all its earnings in

Income War Tax
patronage dividends. It must pay corporation income tax of three per cent of its employed capital. That is perfectly true; the leader of the opposition is right in that. The main purpose of this section is to avoid discrimination between various types of cooperatives, some of which finance on the basis of shares and borrowed money and others of which build up revolving funds or reserves or amounts which have been left without interest, and also to introduce some measure of equity in relation to private businesses which have to raise their capital by paying interest or dividends. That is the purpose of this section. It does not involve large sums jn revenue, but it does preserve a measure of equity between different cooperatives and it does preserve a measure of equity between cooperative enterprise and private business carrying on the same type of activities.
Would not the amount equal to three per cent of the working capital which had been retained from the members be regarded as borrowed capital? As a matter of fact it is; it belongs to the memebrs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would depend on the contract. It might very well be borrowed capital, and the cooperative might enter into an agreement with its members to pay interest on that borrowed' capital. That would be quite permissible.
In which case they would not have to pay the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.
And in which case the leader of the opposition is right?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is right. In that case the three per cent would be deducted as an expense of doing business. But remember that the cooperative or any other organization that borrows money undertakes to pay interest on it and to repay it, and it can be put out of business if it does not pay its debts. That is the difference between an enterprise which has no fixed indebtedness and one which has, and that is an important point to bear in mind in considering these questions. That is another reason for making this distinction.

On section 5, subsection 1-Depreciation.

I believe this is the clause I intended to speak to when I rose before. This has to do with the depreciation
allowance. I would call to the attention of the committee that the previous clause, namely clause 1, allows the minister to give such extra depreciation as the minister in his discretion may allow in the case of plant or equipment built or acquired to fulfil oiders for war purposes. Apparently the present clause is to extend the power of the governor in council to any form of plant or equipment. What I object to in this particular clause is that there is no definition of the different classes. I should think the governor in council could now say on what classes of plant or equipment depreciation would be allowed.
I would point out to the committee that in release No. 14 issued on January 25, 1946, the Department of Reconstruction and Supply
state:
A total of 1,561 applications for "double depreciation" amounting to $244,274,545 have been approved to date by the depreciation committee of the Department of Reconstruction and bupply, Reconstruction Minister Howe said to-day.
The committee was established to considei ap* plications for the depreciation benefits provided by an order in council, P.C. 8640, which grants depreciation to manufacturing industry at from half to double the normal rates for taxation purposes on capital expenditures undertaken in the period from November 10, 1944 to December 31	1946. Such applications must nrst be approved by the committee and by Reconstruction Minister Howe before being passed along to the Donartment of National Revenue.
I should think that the date, December 31, 1946, should read "1945", because this was issued on January 25, 1946. I would, again call attention to the fact that this double depreciation is granted1, notwithstanding the fact that ordinary depreciation must have been taken previously.
Possibly I should have spoken about this matter of depreciation when the other section was before the committee. However, that is passed, and I now say that this is the worst form of paternalism. Some hon. members on this side of the house call it bureaucracy; but I call it paternalism, because the governor in council can actually say, and take the power to say what class should receive this extra benefit. I should think the .minister would hesitate to take upon himself that power- because there will be lots of askers, plenty of people who will ask that they receive double the rates normally allowed.
It has been said that this is done to keep up employment after the war. At the present time there is no lack of employment. Indeed, there is a great lack of all the materials necessary to keep workers employed in build-
Income War Tax

ing. I would say that at this time the measure *is ill-conceived and should not be allowed to operate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The only change made in the present section is to provide that the classes which are to be eligible will be determined by order in council. That, I think, will meet in part the suggestion of the hon, member for Stanstead, namely that they will be specified in the order in council as they are now under the War Measures Act.
Then, on the point raised by the hon. member for High Park, as to whether this is paternalism, my reply would be that I do not know whether it is or not. It is designed to encourage the construction of wealthproducting facilities. One cannot get depreciation more than once. Depreciation of this or any other kind does no more than permit a man to get his capital back. I think it is desirable legislation.
Is it quite clear that plant or equipment includes ships?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It has been so ruled-
I know it has been so ruled.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: -under the present order in council, which is passed under the War Measures Act; and the class or classes will be specified in the new one.

I was wondering if it might not be wise to insert a word which would include ships because, as the minister knows, there have been a number of orders in council passed which apply to ships. It might just be that a great many people would be embarrassed if a court were to determine that the wording did not include ships. If the minister thinks it wise to put in a word to make it clear, it would be helpful.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It has been included in the past; it has been so included in the orders in council. If there is any question of doubt, then I am sure this is a case in which the house would not hesitate to legislate retroactively, if it were thought necessary. But I do not think it is, myself.
Why not obviate that necessity by adding the word "ships".

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not like to include one special type of plant or equipment. This is something which has been in the statute from the beginning. I feel reasonably certain that the department is now allowing double depreciation on ships. That being so, w'ho will question it?

I will just add a word about double depreciation. It has been urged by people who were interested in giving employment, and who also appreciated that costs are extremely 'high at the present time, that it was in the interests of all concerned that this depreciation be granted to encourage the doing now of work which might otherwise be postponed for several years.

The minister promised to give me a definition of "farmer."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

This is important and I want to get to the bottom of it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

In the matter of averaging the income over this triennial period, is account to be taken of the out-of-pocket loss of a taxpayer within this class? Are we to consider only his taxable income, or to permit him to carry into the three-year average the deficit incurred in one year? Take a concrete case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There would be no tax in that year, but a deficit. You go into the three-year average.
Suppose that by reason of losses with his herd he sustained an actual deficit of $2,000. The following year, we will say, he makes a profit of $2,000 and the third year another profit of $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The average income for two years is nil.

Will his income for the three years be the average of $4,000 over three years, or will it be the average of $2,000 on two years? In other words, are you going to allow him to set off the deficit of the first year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The first year he had a loss; [DOT]the second year he had a profit of $2,000, and the third year, another profit of $2,000. The income would be $2,000, averaged over the three years.

I think that is the equitable interpretation, but is that quite what this section says?

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No question about that.
The minister spoke about income in the first year. The department would not call that a deficit; they would just say he earned no income that year.
I want to know where we start this three-year period. Do you start back and go ahead? Do you start this year and then there is next year and the next year ahead, or do you go back?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We start in 1946; that is the first year in which this will apply. The definitive tax payable for 1946, shall I say, will not be ascertained until he knows what his income is for 1948. In 1948 he will average for his three years. If, as a result of that average, he has paid on his actual income in 1946 too much, he has that credit to apply against the tax for 1947 and 1948.
I understand that perfectly, but what about the next year after that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He takes 1947, 1948 and 1949 for his average. It is a moving three-year average. We went into this at some length when we were on the resolution.
That is what I wanted to know.

I tried to reduce it to a set of figures to see if I could get an explanation. In 1946 a farmer has a loss of $4,000; in 1947 he breaks even; in 1948 he has $2,000 taxable income. Then he pays no taxes for those 'hree years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.
Then we go to the next year. In 1947 he breaks even.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.
In 1948 he has shown $2,000. In 1949 he shows $2,500. Then his taxable income is $1,500?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not followed the income figures.
His income for these three years is $4,500?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.
His taxable income would be $1,500?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.

All right. He has not made
any money in those three years, though, if you tax him on the $1,500; he had lost $4,000 in 1946. Can he take that loss of the other $2,000, so that his taxable income would be based on $833 instead of $1,500?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In that case he would be taking the fourth year back for the purpose of his average.
You cannot carry that loss?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No; it is a moving average. You take the taxation year and the two preceding years, beginning in 1946, and then it is a moving average. Once it is established, it keeps moving on forward as long as he is in the business.
That is where the five-year plan would have been better.

I want to come back to the question asked by the hon. member for Eglinton. I have not been able to find in this anything which bears out the explanation which the minister gave. It may be that there is something which makes it applicable, but I am not able to spell it out of the words that any loss would enter in at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The significant words, I think, are "returns of income during the said two preceding years" in line 33 of the section. It is a technical point, but the interpretation which I have given is, I am assured, correct,
Does the income tax return show a deficit? Do you send that in?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Obviously, if you are going to take advantage of the three year averaging you must file a return showing a loss. That will be one of the factors in this new system.

I should like to ask the minister w'hat the position will be if in the next year the farmer receives payment on participation certificates for 1944 and 1945; will he have to credit that income to his 1947 income, or will he be allowed to use it in the years in which it was actually earned? The same will apply -where he receives participation certificates on wheat over the next four years; those participation certificates would be paid in the year 1950, and if they are worth as much as we hope they may be it might mean a considerable income during that year which would have been earned over the other years. Just what is the position?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It goes back to the year of sale. In other words, if the wheat was sold in 1943, and the participation certificate issued is paid in 1945, the payment is taken back into the income of 1943 and the tax adjusted accordingly; and under the section which we shall see a little later there is no interest payable on that additional tax, if any.
Income War Tax

May I ask the minister if this section-which I find it awfully hard to read, containing as it does twenty-three lines without a period, in one sentence-means that the farmer will be able to average his taxes, then average his income and then apply the tax? What is the import of the section?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Average his income.
If he has a loss in one year of $1,000 will that actually apply against the profits of another two years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.
And he averages the income over the moving three-year period and then applies the tax rate against that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.
What is the significance of the first line: "a taxpayer's chief business, occupation, trade or calling"? There are a certain number of people who have other lines of activity.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think it is intended to exclude what I may euphemistically describe as the gentleman farmer who, say, runs a farm as a side-line to his stock or investment brokerage business.
He is on the old basis, is he?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He is on the old basis.

I have got my definition of "farmer", from the note here, but there are a couple of questions I want to get clear in my mind. In Selkirk we have a number of farmer-fishermen; they fish in the winter and farm in the summer. Also we have some farmers who run garages. Will these farmers be able to average their farm incomes over three years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The taxpayer's chief business must be farming or fishing. If he happens to be running a garage on the side that would not affect his status as a farmer or fisherman.
Mr-. BRYCE: A man may be employed in the city and run a fur ranch outside. We have a lot of them around the Red River Valley.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Farming has to be his chief business, occupation or calling to qualify for this special treatment.
And the gentleman who runs a farm as a hobby?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have just answered that question from the hon. member for Rosedale. He does not come under it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have one little technical question. I wonder if the answer the minister give a little while ago was correct or what he intended to give. You are going to average the income of the farmer for the preceding three years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No; the current year and the two preceding years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But he does not pay his tax in the current year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We start in 1946. It will first be ascertained what the average is when the operations for 1948 are concluded.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is neither here nor there, because it is the average for the three years that is taken.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister said that he paid income tax in the fourth year on the basis of the average of those three years. Are you not going to take into account the income tax he has paid in the past three years and bring that into the calculation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are going to take into account the tax paid in the two preceding years when he pays in the third year, and adjust the tax at that time on the basis of the average income for the three years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister will look up the answer he gave the hon. member for Rosedale he will find that he left a different impression. He said the average income, not the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I said that you average the income for the purpose of ascertaining the tax. Then the tax adjustment is merely a matter of mathematics. The tax in the first year may be $1,000 and, in the second year, $1,500. After the third year, the income is averaged and the tax adjustment made on a simple arithmetical basis.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That was not the impression the minister left.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sorry.
What is the position of the farmer who is a member of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think his principal activity is still that of a farmer. He can average his farm income. Of course his income as a member of parliament is constant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
A member of parliament can use his indemnity to pay his losses on- his farm.
[Mr. Abbott.1

War Assets-Army Supplies

I asked the minister earlier if he would not extend the three-year average to five years, and he said he would not do that. I would ask him to reconsider, because I have tables here showing the wheat prices from the year 1910 on, and it shows an erratic picture. I have also a chart showing the yields.
I believe that if the minister would take these tables into consideration he would further consider making it a five-year period instead of a three-year. I move, Mr. Chairman, that subsection 5 of section 8 be amended by striking out the words "forty-eight" in line 77 thereof and substituting therefor the word "fifty", and by striking out the word "two" where it appears in lines 3, 5, 15 and 21 and substituting therefor the word "four." That would mean taking the year 1950 instead of 1948 and making it a five-year average instead of a three-year average.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That, in effect, is the same amendment which my hon. friend moved on the resolution, and I must take the stand I took before that it is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I pointed out on an earlier amendment, the principle of the bill is based on the resolution of the committee of ways and means, and the amendment would disturb the balance of ways and means. It would be out of order at the resolution stage and is equally out of order when the bill is before the committee, and I must so rule.
What is meant by "marine animals" in 'the definition of fishing on page 22?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Seals, I suppose, and that sort of thing. I did not draw the definition. It was intended to be as comprehensive as possible to include the fruits of the sea.

I am not so sure that it includes fish. It says:
"Fishing" includes fishing for or catching shell fish, crustaceans and marine animals.
It seems to include everything but fish. It says "fishing for."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is a legal refinement. The deifinition is intended to expand what might be the ordinary definition of the term "fishing."
I have a question with reference to a growing industry on Vancouver island. Is a man who harvests seaweed a farmer or a fisherman?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
He gets the benefit in either
case.

We have suddenly got away from farming to fishing. I was waiting to put one final word with respect to this farming
proposition which has been mentioned many times in the house. The definition of "farming" is this:
"farming" includes all tillage of the soil, live stock raising, raising of poultry, fur farming, dairying, fruit growing and the keeping of bees.
May I point out that this is work that in the great majority of cases is carried on by the farm family. Yet, as our income tax laws are drafted, one person is taxed on the income earned by the whole family. A large part of this work is done by the women and children of the farmer.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
